articles.title: The Green Agent POV: Formulating the Fix for an Internet-Facing Container with Sensitive Data Access

articles.full_text:
A critical Issue was just discovered in an environment: an internet-facing container running an image with a known initial-access vulnerability, with a role attached that can reach sensitive data.

With AI speed reducing the time from discovery to exploitation, the pressure to fix it fast is intense. Yet remediation is never just about speed. Teams are forced to balance security urgency with business continuity, racing against the clock to answer three critical questions: what’s impacted, what the fix is, and who to send that fix to.

The Wiz Security Graph helps security teams answer the first question. It lays out the exact exposure path including the exposed endpoints, the deployment behind them, the image where the CVE sits, and the lateral movement path that carries an attacker from code execution to buckets holding PII.

Finding the fix and the owner, however, requires deeper investigation that security teams can’t spend hours on. They must rapidly contact the developer to deploy a fix, if it even exists, and apply mitigations in the meanwhile without disrupting production uptime.

That’s what we built Green Agent for. In this post, we’re excited to pull back the curtain and share how Green Agent investigates this exact Issue in minutes and determines the remediation strategies it recommends.

The Investigation

1. Understanding the Issue

Green Agent started by ingesting the Security Graph context to map the full attack path. This Issue represented a toxic combination centered on a single Kubernetes deployment in an AWS EKS cluster.

The Security Graph correlated five distinct risk types converging on this single workload:

External Exposure: A direct network path from the internet to the container.

Vulnerability: A known initial-access CVE-2026-111497 on the container image.

Insecure Kubernetes Cluster: A pod mounting a service account token to bridge into the cloud.

Unprotected Principal: An IAM role granting the workload access to cloud storage.

Unprotected data: Sensitive customer records residing in those accessible buckets.

Five risk types meant five distinct places where the attack chain could be broken - whether by removing the public exposure, patching the container image, unmounting the service account token, scoping down the IAM role, or purging the sensitive data.

Before it could recommend how to break the chain without disrupting production uptime, Green Agent needed to validate the ground truth behind each risk factor. It began investigating the attack path step-by-step, starting at the perimeter.

2. Validating Exposure: Is the Front Door Really Open?

Before recommending a fix, Green Agent needed to determine whether network containment was even an option. Many cloud workloads appear public in configuration tables but are actually shielded behind internal subnets, VPNs, or closed security groups.

Green Agent traced the full inbound route from 0.0.0.0/0:

The Ingress Route: Traffic flowed from the public internet through an AWS Internet Gateway, routed across an AWS Network Load Balancer, passed through the Traefik Ingress controller, and directly into the application's main container.

Unauthenticated Access: Both HTTP (port 80) and HTTPS (port 443) served public endpoints returning unauthenticated 2XX status codes.

No Perimeter Defense: Green Agent inspected the hops and confirmed no Web Application Firewall (WAF) or firewall rules were in place.

This established a critical operational boundary for remediation. Because this frontend was an intentionally public production service, simply pulling the network plug - like tearing down ingress or blocking the load balancer - would cause a total production outage. Any network-level remediation plan from Green Agent would need to preserve uptime, such as introducing authentication middleware rather than severing traffic entirely.

3. Assessing Exploitability: Is the Vulnerability Running in Memory?

With the front door confirmed open, Green Agent moved to the next link in the attack chain: the vulnerability risk factor, to evaluate whether the attack path could be severed at the application layer.

It investigated the container image flaw: CVE-2026-111497 ("Broccoli2Shell"), a critical RCE in the Brotli decoder bundled with Node.js and cataloged in CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV).

It confirmed from the Wiz Sensor that the vulnerable Brotli libraries were actively loaded in memory by the running Node.js process, verifying that code execution was a live, viable threat.

Green Agent also checked upstream advisories and verified that vendor patches (including Node.js 22.23.4 and libbrotli 1.2.1) were already available, confirming a permanent code fix was viable.

However, organizational release processes mean that rolling out a new container image through testing and CI/CD pipelines takes time. Because the attack path can be broken at any of the five risk types, Green Agent turned to the remaining links - the Kubernetes configuration, IAM role, and sensitive data - to see if the toxic combination could be severed immediately in the cloud.

4. Evaluating Cloud Identity & Data: Can the Cloud Path be Severed?

Investigating the workload's connection to cloud storage, Green Agent evaluated the three remaining risk types:

The Cluster Remediation Lever (IRSA): Green Agent examined the Kubernetes service account and confirmed it projected cloud credentials via IRSA into the container. This revealed an immediate mitigation lever: disabling token automount on the pod spec to cut off cloud access.

The IAM Remediation Lever: Inspecting the assumed IAM role, Green Agent found overprivileged s3:GetObject and wildcard s3:* permissions across three S3 buckets. This surfaced a second lever: scoping the IAM policy down to least privilege.

The Data Remediation Lever: Querying the S3 buckets revealed over 5,000 unmasked records (credit cards and PII) in files, identifying a third remediation lever: purging or masking unprotected data at rest.

Investigating these layers proved that Green Agent didn't have to wait on a code deployment to neutralize the risk. Multiple zero-downtime levers were available in the cloud right now.

5. Code-to-Cloud Lineage: Finding the Source and Owners

Cloud mitigations can sever the attack path immediately and buy critical time, but permanent remediation requires fixing at the source. If changes aren't committed to code, the next CI/CD build or Terraform apply will simply overwrite your cloud tweaks and recreate the issue. Green Agent called its Code Subagent to bridge the runtime assets back to version control, tracing the container image to its source Dockerfile, the overprivileged IAM role to its Terraform definitions, and the workload to its GitOps deployment manifests.

By inspecting commit history and metadata, Green Agent connected each fix directly to the engineers who actually maintain the code: the application developer, service owner, and infrastructure lead so security teams didn’t have to go on a search for the right owner.

6. Determining a Verdict and Creating Remediation Plans

Within minutes, Green Agent analyzed organizational context to reach a verdict that this Issue needed to be remediated and is of Critical severity. Green Agent factored in real business impact: the workload belonged to High Business Impact (HBI) production projects, formed an active breach path to 5,000+ sensitive records, and aligned with historical remediation evidence showing 100% of similar sampled issues in the subscription were successfully remediated with a 0% rejection rate.

To break the toxic combination, Green Agent determined that Mitigate and Fix plans were most appropriate to break the risk types identified, balancing immediate protection against permanent resolution:

Mitigate Plans: Immediate actions security teams can deploy right now to reduce the risk, like disabling service account token automount to instantly sever cloud access while developers work on the code fix.

Fix Plans: Permanent root-cause resolutions, like updating the base image in the Dockerfile or scoping down Terraform IAM policies.

Just as importantly, Green Agent evaluated operational trade-offs to skip unviable strategies: it explicitly rejected deleting the ingress because severing an intentionally public frontend would cause a total production outage, and skipped long-term hardening where environment prerequisites weren't in place.

Finally, Green Agent turned planning into execution by assigning each plan directly to its verified owner, ready to resolve via a one-click pull request or by handing instructions straight to a coding agent.

Why this Matters

Green Agent brought two things to this remediation that are notoriously difficult to balance in security: addressing security urgency, and maintaining the context needed to protect business continuity.

First, speed. With risks and threats moving faster than ever, security urgency demands an immediate response. A human team investigating this toxic combination would spend hours or days context-switching: security analysts verifying the public endpoint, platform engineers checking if the Brotli library is actually in memory, cloud admins auditing IAM policies, and developers tracking down which Git repository built the image. Green Agent conducted this investigation in minutes, eliminating the friction and guesswork that typically stalls remediation.

Secondly, operational intelligence. Remediation isn’t only a security team problem, it’s an organizational decision that requires understanding real-world trade-offs. Green Agent knew better than to propose deleting the ingress and taking down a public service that would impact the business. Instead, it distinguished between immediate, zero-downtime cloud mitigations and permanent code fixes, found the exact files in version control, and assigned the work directly to the engineers who own them.

That balance is how organizations can move towards autonomous remediation. Trust has to be earned before teams hand over the keys to auto-execution. That trust is built on context: when engineers see that an agent genuinely understands business trade-offs and won't break production, they can safely evolve from reviewing every action (human-in-the-loop) to supervisory oversight (human-on-the-loop).

That progression is what finally enables teams to get on a path to self-healing, while giving engineers their time back to keep building.

articles.title: ASPM in the AI Era Part 3: Fixing Risk at the Speed of Code
articles.context: True AI threat readiness requires an active ASPM strategy that bridges static code with live cloud context to elevate real, exploitable attack paths over theoretical noise
articles.full_text:
In parts one and two of this series, we covered how to centralize your AppSec tools and use the Wiz Security Graph to isolate critical attack paths. The natural next step to securing your environment is remediating those risks, but for most AppSec teams, fixing vulnerabilities at scale remains a challenge.

Teams invest heavily in SAST, SCA, Secrets, and DAST scanners, only to generate backlogs that stall after triage. According to the Verizon DBIR, unpatched vulnerabilities remain a top attack vector, with organizations taking a median of 47 days to apply a patch, up from 32 days. Those legacy timelines are no longer viable when AI models are compressing the window from vulnerability discovery to active exploitation.

It’s clear the primary bottleneck in AppSec is not finding the risk, but fixing it fast in the code. Driving rapid remediation requires solving three challenges: knowing exactly which developer owns the fix regardless of the scanner, providing them with the precise context needed to execute the fix, and automating that entire workflow at scale.

In this final instalment, we will explore how Wiz Code accelerates remediation and reduces friction for engineering teams:

Simplified ownership mapping: Identifying the right developer to assign remediation tasks to

Deliver agentic, tailored remediation: Generating step-by-step remediation plans and direct pull requests and coding agent handoffs with the Green Agent.

Automate your response: Orchestrating ticketing, developer alerts, and SLA-driven security campaigns via Wiz Workflows.

Remediation Starts with Ownership Mapping

The first major hurdle in remediation is simply knowing who should do the work. In complex enterprise environments, security teams often struggle to map a running cloud vulnerability back to the developer who wrote the original code. Traditional code scanners only see a repository name, branch, or container digest without understanding organizational structure. Teams often manually maintain mappings of Applications to owners, so optimizing this step can significantly deter mean-time-to-remediation (MTTR).

Because of our agentless connection to your Version Control System (VCS), Wiz traces the cloud asset directly back to the specific repository and commit author.

To ensure accuracy, Wiz resolves ownership by correlating multiple data points across your infrastructure. By analyzing resource tags, cloud logs, CMDB data, code commit history, Service Catalog mappings, and Project ownership, the platform routes Issues to the exact person equipped to act on them.

This is the critical first step for the Wiz Green Agent investigation. Before generating a fix, the agent automatically identifies and suggests the most relevant code owner based on your tiered ownership policies.

Tailored Fixes Grounded in Code to Infrastructure Context

Once the right developer is assigned, the next hurdle is actionable guidance. Developers are focused on shipping features, not researching security findings, but in a DevSecOps model, they’re tasked with remediation. Standard fixes from standalone scanners evaluate isolated files and often recommend generic version bumps. The Wiz Green Agent goes beyond generic LLM guidance by providing multi-step remediation plans tailored to your exact environment based on access to the Security Graph.

This includes fixes for Application Security findings surfaced from third party scanners like Snyk, Checkmarx, Semgrep, and more.

Because the agent understands the full code-to-cloud context, it generates a comprehensive plan to eliminate the root cause. For fixes in code, Developers receive two actionable options:

Create a Pull Request: Wiz generates the exact code fix and opens a Pull Request (PR) directly in your repository for the developer to review and merge.

Send to a Coding Agent: Wiz can share the Green Agent’s remediation guidance with an organization's coding agent like a Claude Code to create a PR for a developer to review.

Automate Remediation Playbooks Where Developers Work

Generating a tailored fix is only helpful if the right developer actually sees it. Developers rarely want to log into a dedicated security platform to understand their task backlog, and nothing erodes trust faster than receiving separate tickets for the same finding from different tools. To accelerate remediation, AppSec teams must meet developers in the tools they already use.

This is where Wiz Workflows serves as your automation engine.

Once anIssue is identified and an owner is mapped, Wiz Workflows can automatically route a ticket directly to Jira, ServiceNow, or your supported ITSM platform of choice. You can also configure workflows to send real-time alerts to specific code owners via Slack or Microsoft Teams. Workflows are a powerful system to allow you to coordinate actions across systems (Wiz or external), within customizable, multi-step workflows.

Crucially, these automated tickets include all the original context from your connected third-party scanners alongside the Green Agent's remediation plan. The assigned developer receives the repository details, component versions, vulnerability data, and cloud/runtime context they need. By delivering complete context directly into their native workspace, you eliminate the need for developers to switch between tools to execute a fix.

Moving from Visibility to AI Threat Readiness

In an era where AI accelerates both code generation and exploit velocity, traditional ASPM tools that simply aggregate alerts leave security teams stranded in triage. True AI threat readiness requires an active ASPM strategy that bridges static code with live cloud context to elevate real, exploitable attack paths over theoretical noise.

Wiz Code delivers this complete operational framework by uniting proprietary and third party scanners, Security Graph risk analysis, and agentic remediation into a single platform. By automating the journey from code ownership to verified pull requests, Wiz Code empowers security teams to fix risk at machine speed and stay ahead of modern threats.

articles.title: Critical RCE Vulnerability in Apache HTTP Server: Everything You Need To Know
articles.context: CVE-2026-119618 is a critical, high-severity vulnerability involving a race condition in the Apache HTTP Server, which was independently discovered by Anthropic and Google...
articles.full_text:
A critical synchronization vulnerability (CVE-2026-119618) has been identified in Apache HTTP Server’s HTTP/2 module (mod_http2). The flaw stems from a concurrent execution race condition within the assign_headers() function when handling shared resources. If successfully exploited, a remote, unauthenticated attacker can corrupt heap memory to achieve arbitrary code execution (RCE).

As of the time of this blog’s publication, no exploit is available and there are no reports of exploitation in the wild.

What is CVE-2026-111497?

CVE-2026-119618 is a critical, high-severity vulnerability involving a race condition in the Apache HTTP Server, which was independently discovered by Anthropic and Google Cloud’s Vulnerability Research Team.

Specifically, the flaw exists within the assign_headers() function of the HTTP/2 module (mod_http2). Due to improper synchronization when executing concurrent threads sharing resources, an attacker can trigger heap corruption. This memory corruption can ultimately be leveraged to achieve RCE on the hosting server, allowing unauthorized threat actors to execute arbitrary commands with the privileges of the web server process.

Wiz Research data: what’s the risk to cloud environments?

In cloud environments, a compromised Apache instance running containerized or virtualized workloads can serve as an entry point for lateral movement, potentially exposing adjacent microservices or cloud metadata endpoints.

According to Wiz data 64% of cloud environments have resources vulnerable to CVE-2026-119618, and 51% of cloud environments have publicly exposed instances. Note that this does not take configuration into account.

Which products are affected?

The vulnerability affects deployments utilizing HTTP/2 capabilities on the Apache HTTP Server within the version ranges outlined in the table below:

Vendor

Product

Affected Versions

Patched Versions

Apache Software Foundation

Apache HTTP Server

From 2.4.55 through 2.4.70

2.4.71 and newer

GitHub (Open Source)

mod_h2 module

From 2.0.8 through 2.0.42

2.0.24 and newer

Which actions should security teams take?

Security operations and engineering teams should execute the following remediation and mitigation steps:

1. Upgrade Deployments

Upgrade Apache HTTP Server: Update affected installations to Apache HTTP Server version 2.4.71 or later. This release addresses the race condition in assign_headers().

Update Standalone Modules: If managing standalone mod_h2 builds from GitHub, upgrade the module to a version newer than 2.0.42.

2. Implement Temporary Mitigations

If immediate patching is not possible due to operational constraints, temporarily disable HTTP/2 support to eliminate the attack vector.

Edit the configuration file (such as httpd.conf) to restrict active protocols to HTTP/1.1 by removing h2 and h2c references:

# Restrict protocols to HTTP/1.1 Protocols http/1.1

Wiz customers can use the pre-built query and advisory in the Wiz Threat Center to search for vulnerable instances in their environment.

articles.title: How to Evaluate AI Agent Cybersecurity Capabilities
articles.context: Many companies already use agents within their development and deployment ecosystem, and attackers sometimes use swarms of offensive agents to attack thousands of companies at once
articles.full_text:
How do you measure the success with which different agents perform regular, real-world cybersecurity tasks?

Many companies already use agents within their development and deployment ecosystem, and attackers sometimes use swarms of offensive agents to attack thousands of companies at once. To help defenders prepare for this new era, we need a score that compares what these agents can do. Because of how important this is, labs in academia across the industry are starting to work on measuring it and setting a standard for how to do it correctly, so the topic is timely and increasingly relevant.

In this post I’ll share the key principles Wiz followed to tackle this benchmarking imperative in the relaunch of our Cyber Model Arena. The full methodology, how we graded, and gathered our tasks is available for download. As of the writing of this blog, the Wiz Cyber Model Arena v3.9 consists of 26 models, four general-purpose harnesses, 59 agents, 327 challenges, three attempts per challenge, and 1,000 seconds each (these numbers are constantly growing).

To create a benchmark, fix the benchmark objective first. Then build the tasks, environment, and the measurement around it. I’ll get into this and explain the principles that guide the process, in greater detail later in this post.

Key Takeaways

Choose the right tasks. Settle the why (objective), the what (data, ground truth and agent setup) and the how (metrics, evaluation function) before you write the first task. Build the data from the real distribution where you can, not from AI-generated or AI-labeled tasks.

Grade with code, not LLMs. Measure success directly and deterministically, and apply anti-cheat measures: isolate the agent from the server and the internet, and give it no way to look up answers. Do not rely on an LLM-as-a-judge unless it is well designed, calibrated and free of bias.

Optimize evaluation for realism. Evaluate the harness and model together, give the agent more than one try, and weigh success against what a solve costs.

Avoid common pitfalls. LLM judges, small samples, task imbalance, model-only evaluation and answer leakage each make a benchmark unreliable. And start small: one harness, a quick and cheap model, a few tasks and a simple grader. Scale only after it works.

Start with a problem statement

Most public cyber-agent benchmarks answer a different question than the one a defender is asking. A multiple-choice quiz benchmark measures model knowledge not production performance, and an LLM output judged by another model measures agreement between the two, not success. We aim to answer whether the agent can perform a real attack.

Write down the one question your benchmark must answer, and test every later decision against it. Ours:

Given only the task instruction, a general-purpose agent scaffold, a 1,000-second budget, and no external knowledge sources, does the agent produce a checkable effect on a real target?

Wiz Research's 2026 State of AI in the Cloud Report found that at least 57% of organizations have deployed self-hosted AI agent technology, and that MCP servers appear in at least 80% of observed cloud environments. People are already buying and defending against these systems. That is the why. The rest of this post is how to build a number that serves it.

Design your benchmark

Define three things before you create your first challenge.

Why. A defender or a buyer should be able to act on the number. "Higher pass@1" is not a why. "Can this agent, as shipped, exploit a live target from the instruction alone?" is.

What. Name the subject under evaluation. Here it is an agent (model + harness + tools + system prompt) run by an attacker, which is why we use realistic limits: 1,000 seconds, three attempts, a simple system prompt, and access to client-side code but not server-side code.

How. It’s important for the benchmark to report a single bottom line metric per example. To reduce many competing metrics to a single number, pick one optimizing metric and treat everything else as a satisficing constraint. If you have five competing metrics and no way to reduce them, which agent is better becomes a debate over the metrics.

Make the tasks match the job

A benchmark can only speak for the tasks it contains. Sample only the hard tasks and you are no longer measuring success on the job, you are measuring success on hard tasks. And a benchmark that claims to measure "offensive capability" from a single task category oversells itself.

So we built four categories of equal weight from sources that already exist in the wild. We did not generate or label tasks with an LLM.

Category

Tasks

What it tests

Code vulnerabilities

221

Finding known vulnerabilities in stripped open-source packages, or exploiting a live 1-day CVE

API security

54

Attacking black-box APIs with no source code

Web security

29

Exploiting real PHP web apps with the client source visible

Cloud security

23

Exploiting misconfigurations across AWS, Azure, GCP and Kubernetes-style setups

The agents behave very differently from one category to the next. Averaged over the 59 agents, pass@1 is 78.0% on API security, 64.6% on web, 56.5% on cloud and 38.2% on code vulnerabilities. The top overall agent scores 74.7% on web and 65.8% on code (while web tops out at 90.8%). Another agent scores 9.7% on code and still 71.6% on API.

Size matters too. Many recent cybersecurity benchmarks have fewer than 30 tasks. At a 50% success rate, 30 tasks give a 95% confidence interval of roughly ±18 points, so an agent that scores 15 points higher than another is not necessarily better.

Grade an effect, not with LLMs

Ground truth is the foundation of evaluation. It has been standard practice to grade with an LLM-as-a-Judge, but judges do not directly measure success. They are biased (they often prefer the first option), random (they give different results each run), expensive, and slow, and they must be calibrated and de-biased before you can use them in a long-lived benchmark. When you use a judge, you measure whether an LLM thinks the agent succeeded. That difference is a debt baked into the system.

We use code instead. Every challenge is designed to leave a checkable effect behind or report precise structured outputs, and a deterministic grader inspects it after the agent is gone. Code graders are cheap, re-runnable, and not a model you have to calibrate.

Anti-cheating via isolation

Agents will shortcut a task when they can. They look the answer up online, read a solution off disk, or manipulate the grader. A score collected with web search, a CVE database or the challenge name in the folder measures something else: success at the task or success at breaking it. CTFusion moved their solve rate by as much as 12 points just by raising web-search access.

As for contamination, we cannot prove our agents never saw a task in pretraining. We can prove they cannot fetch one during the trial. Anti-cheat belongs in the environment, not in the prompt.

Start small

Building a benchmark is a nontrivial, evolving effort, and it is tempting to write 300 challenges before anything runs end to end. We apply lean-startup rules instead: get a small end-to-end baseline you can inspect by hand, then iterate.

You need ten tasks you can re-run, one harness you can deploy, and an evaluation metric a grader can check. After you’re convinced it works, you can scale it up.

What we found

Pair the harness with the model

A model on its own is a text predictor. It becomes an attacker inside a harness that runs commands and applies tools, and models do better or worse in different harnesses. Across the 22 models we ran on both Claude Code and ADK React, the mean absolute gap was 5.1 pass@1 points. Claude models prefer Claude Code, and Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber prefers the thinner ADK loop.

The conclusion: test the system as a whole. Either pair the harness to the model (and as we’ve seen it’s best to match the harness to the model's creator), or fix one general harness and compare models inside it.

Attackers get more than one try

A real attacker does not stop after one failure. We gave every agent three attempts per challenge, and the extra attempts did more than lift scores. For some agents they even changed which one comes out ahead.

Accuracy has a price

Give an agent more time and money and it will usually solve more. So the useful chart plots success against what a solve costs. Any agent off the Pareto frontier is strictly worse than one on it. For example, Claude Code with GPT-5.6 Sol averages 64.2% pass@1 at $8.29 and 27.2 minutes per solve, however the Pareto frontier Codex + GPT-6 Luna is strictly better, averaging 64.5% pass@1 at only $0.05 and 6.3 minutes per solve.

Keep a short list of agents on the frontier and ignore the rest. That lets you ask "for this budget, how do I maximize success?" or "for this success rate, how do I minimize cost?"

Limitations

Four simple harnesses. A cyber-specialized harness would likely score higher, but we chose to measure a simple attacker.

String equality on code vulnerabilities. A semantically correct root cause that misses the expected symbol scores 0. We chose precision over recall.

Public web tasks. websec.fr is a known corpus. Isolation stops the agent from looking up the answer, not from remembering it from training (possibly resulting in benchmark contamination).

A time cap. 1,000 seconds is enough for most successful attacks we observed. In the future we think it is better to limit cost than time.

Confidence intervals. We have yet to publish them on the website, and we are working on it.

Conclusion

Our Cyber Model Arena shows how different agents perform on common cybersecurity tasks, across 327 isolated challenges in four categories. To build an agentic cybersecurity benchmark, fix the why, the what and the how first, and define the agent, the task mix, the grader, the isolation, the budget and the attempts. Get one wrong and the benchmark becomes garbage in, garbage out.

Appendix: Results for All 59 Agents

Every agent, ordered by pass@1. Scores are percentages.

Source: Wiz Cyber Model Arena v3.9.

Wiz and ISMAP: How We Are Preparing to Serve Japan's Public Sector

When Japanese government agencies procure cloud services, they are required, in principle, to procure from services registered on the ISMAP Cloud Service List. This list is established under ISMAP (Information system Security Management and Assessment Program), in accordance with the "Common Standards for Cybersecurity Measures for Government Agencies and Related Agencies. ISMAP is a framework that evaluates and registers cloud services in advance to ensure they satisfy the security requirements mandated by the government.

Without an active ISMAP listing, Japanese government agencies face a barrier to adoption. While Wiz is not listed on ISMAP yet, we're actively working through the controls and wanted to share where we actually stand today.

What ISMAP Is, and Why It Matters

In practice, ISMAP gives procurement officers a pre-vetted catalog of cloud providers. Getting onto that list comes with strict baseline demands:

Mandatory external audits conducted by audit firms registered on the ISMAP Auditors List

Japanese-language application support, along with the preparation of documentation and audit trails required for review and examination

Post-registration adherence to scheduled renewal applications and ongoing audits and verifications

Under the hood, ISMAP complements established global standards. The ISMAP Control Measures are built around the Common Standards for Government Agencies as well as JIS Q 27001 and JIS Q 27017, the Japanese national standards for ISO/IEC 27001 and ISO/IEC 27017, covering information security management and cloud security controls. While ISMAP aligns with these frameworks, holding these certifications does not directly equate to ISMAP registration. Additionally, ISMAP also pulls in ISO/IEC 27018 for cloud privacy, alongside NIST SP 800-53 controls to plug edge cases that the core ISO standards do not explicitly cover.

Currently, proposed revisions to the ISMAP Control Measures have been published, focusing on reflecting revised international standards and streamlining the number of control measures. These proposals aim to reorganize and rationalize the control system, which is expected to enhance efficiency upon revision and enforcement while maintaining the security and reliability demanded by the program. Please note that the draft revisions and implementation schedule remain subject to change.

Where Wiz Stands Today

Wiz has maintained active ISO 27001, ISO 27017, ISO 27018, SOC 2, PCI DSS, and FedRAMP certifications and reports for the past five years. Our commitment to compliance gives our teams established practices for control implementation, evidence collection, and continuous audit readiness. We recently finished an internal gap assessment against both the current ISMAP Control Measures and the published revision proposals to prepare for the upcoming ISMAP audit.

To address the specific requirements of the ISMAP framework, we are actively building out the localized evidence packages and formal processes required for ISMAP assessors. In parallel, we have engaged with an audit firm registered on the ISMAP Auditors List, with target plans to formally launch the external assessment audit in early 2027.

What This Means for Customers

To be clear: ISMAP does not offer an official "in progress" or provisional status. You're either on the official registry or you are not–and right now, we are not.

What we can confirm is that we are executing our ISMAP-specific requirements by leveraging our extensive experience with certifications such as ISO 27001, SOC 2 Type II, PCI-DSS, FedRAMP, IRAP, and CPSTIC. We have completed the gap analysis, engaged with registered assessors, and are addressing control artifacts ahead of time rather than scrambling during the audit window.

In the meantime, security teams in Japan already use Wiz to audit and enforce the core security areas: IAM, data encryption, centralized logging, continuous vulnerability scanning, and incident response. However, compliance with ISMAP security standards is not verified or guaranteed solely by the use of Wiz.

Looking Ahead

Our roadmap is straightforward: finalize the contract with an assessment body and formally commence the external ISMAP assessment audit in early 2027. We will share further updates as we hit key audit milestones over the next year.

If you are navigating Japanese public sector compliance today, we can walk you through our current security posture, share our active ISO and SOC 2 reports, and show you how our existing control mapping aligns with ISMAP. Reach out to your Wiz account team or contact us directly.

articles.title: Trusted by Default: Qubole Cross-Account Access Abused in the Wild
articles.context: Once inside multiple victim AWS environments, the threat actor enumerated resources, collected configuration and secrets, accessed S3 data, and validated additional credentials...
articles.full_text:
Third-party integrations are one of the most common ways organizations grant outside parties access to their cloud environments. Working with Sentra and Mandiant, Wiz observed a threat actor using IAM credentials from an AWS account associated with Qubole between October 14 and October 26, 2026. The actor used these credentials to assume IAM roles that customers had created to trust Qubole's account. Once inside multiple victim AWS environments, the threat actor enumerated resources, collected configuration and secrets, accessed S3 data, and validated additional credentials it discovered along the way.

Sentra identified suspicious activity across several of their customer environments, recognized it as a broad supply chain attack, and shared the information with Wiz, prompting this investigation. This post describes what Wiz observed, how defenders can hunt for it, and how to reduce exposure from third-party cross-account trust relationships. Wiz customers can refer to our Threat Intel Center advisory for this activity.

Background: How Cross-Account Vendor Access Works

Many SaaS platforms that operate inside a customer's AWS account, including data processing platforms like Qubole, use cross-account IAM roles. During onboarding, the customer creates a role in their own account with a trust policy that allows the vendor's AWS account to assume it, typically gated by an External ID:

{ "Effect": "Allow", "Principal": { "AWS": "arn:aws:iam::<vendor-account-id>:root" }, "Action": "sts:AssumeRole", "Condition": { "StringEquals": { "sts:ExternalId": "<external-id>" } } }

When the vendor needs to act in the customer's environment, an identity in the vendor's account calls sts:AssumeRole with the role ARN and External ID, and receives temporary credentials scoped to the customer's role.

What We Observed

Initial Access: Role Assumption from the Vendor Account

The first activity Wiz CIRT observed occurred on October 14, when an IP address belonging to Mullvad VPN (45.83.220[.]211) called AssumeRole against integration roles in customer environments. The calls originated from AWS account 805246085872, which we observe Qubole's platform using to assume roles in customer environments, and used the IAM user AIDA3W7DIFLYOLTK63SFS. Across the affected environments, Wiz CIRT has not observed this IAM user in any activity other than that associated with this threat actor.

From October 15, most of the activity came from a VPS hosted by OVH (57.129.54[.]120). On October 18, the threat actor began using a second IAM user from the same account, AIDAJYRRH5Y3A7AAJM2HW, which also carries legitimate Qubole platform traffic from AWS infrastructure. The same day, a second Mullvad address (185.209.199[.]73) assumed integration roles across multiple victim environments in quick succession. Every AssumeRole request we attributed to the threat actor included an External ID, and every one succeeded.

Most of the roles the threat actor assumed were not otherwise in use. In a majority of the environments Wiz CIRT observed, the threat actor's requests were the only AssumeRole activity from the vendor account in October. The trust policies were still in place, so the requests succeeded.

Discovery

The threat actor used role session names that followed a consistent format of the prefix quiam-, followed by a suffix describing the actions taken. This includes session names such as quiam-enum and quiam-scope-full.

Once inside an environment, the threat actor enumerated broadly across services. Including:

Storage and data: ListBuckets, ListObjects, GetDatabases, ListTables, DescribeClusters

Compute: DescribeInstances, DescribeImages, DescribeSecurityGroups, DescribeVpcs

Databases: DescribeDBInstances, DescribeDBSnapshots

Identity and keys: ListRoles, ListKeys, ListAliases, DescribeKey, GetKeyPolicy

Credential Harvesting and Secret Validation

The threat actor targeted common places where credentials are stored in AWS:

Lambda: the threat actor listed Lambda functions and called GetFunctionConfiguration on each, which returns function environment variables.

Secrets Manager: ListSecrets followed by GetSecretValue

SSM Parameter Store: DescribeParameters and GetParameter.

The threat actor used TruffleHog to test credentials it found in victim environments. These belonged to the affected organizations, not to the vendor:

AWS: TruffleHog called GetCallerIdentity with discovered IAM user access keys. The call needs no permissions and confirms whether a key is valid. The threat actor checked keys from several AWS accounts in bursts lasting seconds.

Entra ID: TruffleHog signed in as Entra ID service principals using discovered client secrets.

Okta: TruffleHog requested OAuth tokens using discovered Okta client credentials.

Data Access and Exfiltration

Using the assumed integration roles, the threat actor exfiltrated data from S3. The sequence was consistent across environments: assume a role, call ListBuckets to see what the role could reach, call ListObjects and HeadObject to enumerate and inspect the contents, then call GetObject to download them. The threat actor appears to have been opportunistic. Rather than looking for specific data, it read from whatever buckets each role could reach, in some cases downloading entire buckets in a single session.

To detect this kind of exfiltration, organizations should make sure S3 data events in CloudTrail or S3 server access logs are enabled for buckets that hold sensitive data. CloudTrail management events record the role assumption and the bucket listing, but not the object reads that make up the data exfiltration.

.iso Image Hints At Additional Operations

In addition to the intrusions above, Wiz Research identified, via Validin, an ISO file that was hosted on the 57.129.54[.]120 IP address during the time it was controlled by the threat actor. This file, sso_agent.iso, (SHA-256 65f061281c9a712e9502793dc4c5035cae490b84da05f7d4223cefa65ad396e4) is a bootable linux image that we believe is designed to be remotely booted on a victim machine. When the iso is started it begins a 90 minute clock, gathers system information and uploads interfaces and disk and partition lists to the 57.129.54[.]120 IP address. It then polls the same IP address via TCP port 23458 for input and runs it as a shell script. This polling continues until the 90 minute timer is up when a hard reboot is triggered, erasing any evidence of the malicious iso. While the polling command can run any script sent to it, the iso is set to load the ntfs3 driver at boot, suggesting that it is designed to target windows operating systems.

Wiz has not identified any deployments of this iso and cannot confirm if or how it has been used.

Attribution and Motivation

Wiz has not identified any ties between this campaign and other publicly reported activity. The targeting and data theft appear opportunistic and do not match typical state-backed priorities; however we don’t have any direct insight into the motivation of the threat actor or how they may use the stolen data.

Additional Qubole Related Activity

Wiz also identified a separate set of malicious activity involving Qubole integrations. We have not been able to link it to the role assumption activity described above.

From October 8 to October 11, an actor used customer-owned AWS access keys that we believe were created for Qubole integrations. On October 8, the actor tested all of these keys within a single hour. In a small number of cases, the actor went on to compromise the victim's cloud environment.

Detection and Hunting

Organizations that have integrated with Qubole should review CloudTrail from October 1, 2026 onward, in every account that holds an integration role:

AssumeRole events where userIdentity.accountId is 805246085872 and sourceIPAddress is not an AWS address. All legitimate platform traffic we observed came from AWS infrastructure.

AssumeRole events where userIdentity.principalId is AIDA3W7DIFLYOLTK63SFS. In the environments we observed, only the threat actor used this IAM user, so any activity from it warrants investigation.

AssumeRole events where userIdentity.principalId is AIDAJYRRH5Y3A7AAJM2HW and sourceIPAddress is not an AWS address. This IAM user also carries legitimate platform traffic from AWS infrastructure, so filter on the source address to separate the threat actor's use from normal activity.

Any activity from the IP addresses in the IOC tables below. The Mullvad addresses are shared VPN exit nodes, so activity from them alone is not conclusive.

GetCallerIdentity calls with a TruffleHog user agent paired with any IOC IP address, which show the credentials the threat actor tried to validate. Check your identity provider's sign-in logs for the same user agent.

For every role session you find, review all subsequent activity from that session, especially Secrets Manager, SSM Parameter Store, Lambda and S3. If the threat actor assumed an integration role, rotate every secret, parameter and Lambda environment variable the role could read, and revoke active sessions for the role. Rotating a credential does not end temporary sessions that were already issued.

Wiz Defend customers ingesting CloudTrail will see Wiz Threats for IAM Role Assumed From New or Inactive Account and Unusual non-human access to AWS through third-party VPN.

Recommendations for Defenders

Inventory third-party trust relationships. Identify every IAM role whose trust policy allows an external account. Wiz customers can use the Security Graph to list roles that trust external AWS accounts, along with the permissions and data those roles can reach. [Security Graph Query]

Remove trust for integrations you no longer use. Many victim environments had no legitimate vendor traffic during this activity. Those roles still accepted the threat actor's requests. Delete integration roles you no longer use, or remove the vendor account from their trust policies.

Narrow the trusted principal. Where the vendor supports it, replace the account :root principal with the specific IAM principal the vendor uses. Add an aws:SourceIp or aws:SourceVpce condition that limits role assumption to the vendor's documented network ranges. With these conditions in place, a valid External ID from an unexpected identity or network is rejected. In this activity, a source IP condition alone would have blocked every role assumption we observed.

Treat the External ID as non-secret. It is logged in plaintext in CloudTrail and is often stored by the vendor and in infrastructure-as-code. Don't rely on it as the only control. After an event like this, rotate it in coordination with the vendor, and use a distinct value per role where supported.

Limit what integration roles can reach. Review the permissions attached to vendor roles. Access to Lambda configuration, Secrets Manager, SSM parameters and broad S3 read is often granted for convenience. Ensure the principle of least privilege is followed.

Alert on third-party role assumption from new networks. Vendor traffic usually comes from a known set of cloud networks. An AssumeRole from a vendor account through a VPN or a hosting provider the vendor has never used is a high-signal detection.

Make sure your logs cover every account. Use an organization trail that covers all accounts and regions, and enable S3 data events or S3 server access logs for sensitive buckets. In several affected environments, missing logs meant responders could not see which S3 objects the threat actor read.

SaaS providers, lock down the principals your customers trust. Customers extend trust to the principals in your account, so those principals are effectively credentials to every customer environment at once. Assume customer roles from workload roles with short-lived credentials rather than long-lived IAM user keys, restrict where those principals can be used with aws:SourceIp or aws:SourceVpc conditions, publish your egress ranges so customers can pin their trust policies, and monitor your own CloudTrail for AssumeRole calls into customer accounts from unexpected networks.

articles.title: The ROI of Agentic Remediation: Real-World Results with Wiz Green Agent
articles.context: When an active zero-day like the recent PHP2Shell vulnerability breaks, security tools light up within minutes, flagging critical production risks that demand an immediate fix
articles.full_text:
When an active zero-day like the recent PHP2Shell vulnerability breaks, security tools light up within minutes, flagging critical production risks that demand an immediate fix. And while AI has accelerated how quickly vulnerabilities are discovered, fixing them still waits on human coordination.

However, implementing that fix extends far beyond the security team and becomes an organization-wide initiative. Security teams discover the risk, but they don't own the code, the infrastructure, or the deployment pipelines. Resolving the issue requires coordinating across three distinct teams, each with their own set of priorities:

Security: Wants to eliminate exploitable risk immediately.

Engineering: Wants to maintain shipping velocity without breaking dependencies or spending time figuring out the right fix.

Cloud / Platform Operations: Wants to preserve uptime and infrastructure stability.

With each team working in their own workflows and against their own roadmap, remediation becomes an expensive game of cross-departmental ping pong. Tickets bounce between teams, developers waste hours determining the environment-specific fix, and Mean Time to Remediation (MTTR) grows.

To close this gap, organizations need a bridge between runtime context and developer execution so fixing becomes automated and continuous. Here is how leading teams use Wiz Green Agent to eliminate the three core bottlenecks of remediation, the ROI they achieve, and how that work builds towards a self healing cloud.

The Three Bottlenecks that make remediation hard

Finding the right owner for the Issue

Before a team can investigate or fix a risk, they run into the first hurdle: who actually owns the vulnerable asset? In dynamic multi-cloud, hybrid, or AI environments, that answer is hard to come by. A production container might have been deployed through a shared pipeline, authored by an engineer who switched teams months ago, or spun up across accounts with missing tags and with a CMDB that’s out of date. When ownership isn't clear, Issues sit unassigned in backlog queues or bounce between Platform, DevOps, and AppSec teams trying to determine whose repo or service an issue belongs to.

That delay in finding an owner stretches out remediation cycles before work can even begin.

How Green Agent solves it

Green Agent eliminates the ownership guessing game by connecting signals from across your entire environment. By analyzing repository commit history, Wiz Project assignments, service catalogs, CMDB integrations, and cloud logs, Green Agent automatically identifies the Suggested Assignee: the specific developer or individual best positioned to act.

Security teams can assign the issue to the right owner with one click directly inside the Issue drawer, ensuring Issues land with the person who can actually merge the fix.

This analysis is how teams like Rogo, an enterprise AI platform for financial institutions, eliminate manual cross-team detective work while maintaining rapid development velocity across AWS and GCP:

With the Green Agent it's surfaced automatically in the Wiz Issue and is incredibly valuable in finding the right person so our developers can quickly remediate.

Eric Tu, Product Security Engineer, Rogo

Understanding risk at the root cause

When a critical security Issue hits a developer’s queue, they want clear, actionable answers on what they need to fix, where it lives in code, and how they need to fix it so they can get back to shipping new features. Getting to those answers starts with tracing it back from runtime to code to understand the root cause.

That means confirming the workload is actually exposed, verifying the vulnerable package is reachable, and locating the originating repository, Dockerfile, or commit that introduced it. Doing that forensic legwork by hand for every alert is slow and repetitive, and at cloud scale, with AI pushing more code into production every week, it's where the bulk of triage time goes before the fix can begin.

How Green Agent solves it

Green Agent automates that entire investigation under the hood. For each Issue, it reasons across the Wiz Security Graph to evaluate runtime exposure, identity access, and code-to-cloud mapping to understand the root cause. It confirms whether the risk is truly exploitable and recommends whether to remediate or adjust the severity to keep developers focused on high-priority risks, then pinpoints the exact file and line in the source code responsible for the vulnerability.

As a result of Green Agent’s AI investigation engine, Fireblocks, the digital asset and blockchain infrastructure provider, cut daily operational triage time by more than 70% and now reaches same-day resolution on critical risks.

Green Agent explains the full context; it shows us all of our workloads and the exact remediation path for any issue. All the remediation paths are really clear... Before Red Agent, Green Agent, and the Cloudflare integration, we used to have manual processes for triage. Now, we get clearer findings and faster remediation that reduce the amount of manual hours of operation needed.

Roy Weiss, Principal DevSecOps, Fireblocks

Turning alerts into actionable fixes for developers

Even with the right owner assigned and the root cause identified, the final friction point is execution: turning that Issue into merged code.

Handing an engineer an alert with a link to a generic CVE bulletin forces them to context-switch away from their sprint, research potential patches, and figure out how to write the fix without breaking existing dependencies. Developers are focused on building and shipping product features; for remediation to move at the speed of AI engineering, the specific environmental fix has to meet developers directly in their everyday workflows.

How Green Agent solves it

Green Agent closes that loop by generating prescriptive, environment-specific remediation. It provides code or Terraform changes needed down to the exact line, and surfaces 1-click Pull Requests or handoffs to coding agents so developers can simply review, validate, and merge. For teams building with AI, Green Agent also exposes its remediation context via API and the Wiz Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, allowing developers to pull Green Agent’s remediation recommendations directly inside their agentic IDEs to accelerate fixing.

By meeting developers where they work and removing the manual research burden, project44, the global supply chain visibility platform, accelerated their remediation velocity by 10x while keeping engineering focused on roadmap priorities:

AI has enhanced coding velocity for engineers; the Green Agent from Wiz offers a similar increase in velocity for security engineering work.

Matthew Blackert, Security Operations Manager, project44

Our Wiz enablement with Engineering showed us what's possible when you remove the noise: engineers fixing real risk instead of validating false positives.

Mihajlo Jankovic, Security Operations Analyst II, project44

Closing the Remediation Gap

Remediation speed is no longer limited by how fast security can find risks, it’s defined by how smoothly security context converts into developer action.

By eliminating the context gap, automating ownership attribution, and delivering 1-click code fixes, Wiz Green Agent transforms remediation from a cross-team tax into an automated, closed-loop workflow.

articles.title: From Reactive to Proactive: Empowering SOC Teams with the Wiz Red and Blue Agents
articles.context: Agentic security for the SOC: proactive first, defensive always Detection still matters, but it shouldn't be the first time you hear about a critical, validated, exploitable risk
articles.full_text:
Most SOC teams start investigating when a threat alert fires. Analysts triage the alert, piece together context, and begin an investigation, all after something has already happened. That model was built for a world where attackers moved at human speed and relied mostly on known exploits.

That's no longer the case. Two shifts are happening at the same time, and both are changing the day-to-day for the SOC:

• Organizations are shipping more custom code than ever: AI-assisted development means teams are building custom AI applications at unprecedented speed. These apps can contain logic-driven vulnerabilities, such as broken authorization and authentication bypasses, that are impossible to detect with signature-based scanners.

• Attackers are using AI to move faster: Adversaries are using frontier AI models to scan perimeters, find exposed applications, and weaponize vulnerabilities in hours instead of months. AI also lowers the barrier to entry, so more attackers can probe custom applications for weaknesses, at greater scale than ever.

For the SOC, that means the first sign of a logic flaw is often the breach itself. By the time a detection fires, the attacker has already chained their way in.

Human-speed defense can't keep up with AI-powered offense. The only way to keep pace is to use AI to fight AI: find the open door before an attacker walks through it, and investigate at AI speed when someone does. This is critical for incident response in the AI era, and ensuring that the SOC can action at the speed required to defend the enterprise.

Proactive security belongs in the SOC

Gartner® makes the priority clear:

Proactive, continuous threat exposure management (CTEM) with offensive testing will dominate SOC operations, as reactive detection yields an exponential increase in diminishing returns.

Gartner Report, The Security Operations Roadmap to 2030, By Kevin Schmidt, Alex Tytarenko, etc., October 2026. Gartner is a trademark of Gartner, Inc. and/or its affiliates

For the SOC, this means treating validated, exploitable exposures as what they are: attack paths that are proven exploitable. They deserve the same urgency as an active threat, because in the AI era, it's only a matter of time before attackers find them.

That is the job of two Wiz agents working together:

• The Red Agent, our AI-powered attacker that continuously finds and validates exploitable risk across your attack surface, and delivers it as pre-breach, SOC-level alerts.

• The Blue Agent, our AI investigator that works alongside analysts to investigate active threats with full cloud, code, and runtime context, and reach a confident verdict fast.

Red Agent: Pre-breach alerts your SOC can trust

The Red Agent is an AI-powered pentester that enables teams to uncover complex, validated exploitable risks and remove them before attackers find them, at machine speed. It works alongside Wiz ASM to cover all types of risks- from known risks, such as CVEs and misconfigurations, to the unknown, logic-based risks in custom-built applications, like authorization bypasses that signature-based scanners miss.

Every validated exploitable risk Red Agent finds is a ticking time bomb. Red Agent has already proven the exploit works, so the only open question is who gets there next: your team or an attacker. That calls for pre-breach urgency, not a place in the vulnerability backlog.

Each finding arrives with proof of exploitability, reproduction steps, blast radius context from the Security Graph, and a clear owner and remediation guidance from the Green Agent. Instead of waiting for a detection, teams can shut down the attack path first and respond to fewer incidents.

What is most amazing about Red Agent is the way that we can track and get alerting or visibility on endpoints that can be attacked or manipulated from the outside. It tells me: 'You have an endpoint here, you are missing authentication, you have an exposure.' All of those insights are really, really helping me to close gaps fast.

Roy Weiss, Principal DevSecOps, Fireblocks

What a pre-breach SOC alert looks like

In one finding from our Red Agent POV series, Red Agent found a way into a financial services company's production cloud API without authentication, exposing live cloud credentials and the application's full source code.

Without Red Agent, the SOC might first learn about this risk when those credentials are used from an unfamiliar location, and only then start investigating what the attacker touched. With Red Agent, the SOC can act before an attacker finds it, and close the door on what would have been a breach before it can begin.

The pre-breach playbook

When Red Agent finds a validated exploitable risk, here's a playbook the SOC can follow. The steps will feel familiar from incident response, but they happen before a breach instead of after one. Here's how it works for this example:

1. Triage: already done. Red Agent proved the path is exploitable and provides reproduction steps. There's no "is this real?" debate.

2. Scope: has anyone already used this path? Threat hunters check whether a real attacker got there first. Here, that means assuming and looking for any use of the exposed credentials from unexpected sources.

3. Contain: put a stopgap in place. Rotate the credentials and restrict the endpoint. That buys time before the permanent fix.

4. Hand off: Green Agent routes the fix. The Green Agent identifies who owns the affected application and sends them specific fix guidance, so nobody has to hunt for the owner.

5. Verify: Confirm the path is closed. Once the owner ships the fix, Red Agent retests the same exploitable risk to confirm it no longer works.

Blue Agent: AI investigation for active threats

Proactive alerts shrink the attack surface, but no SOC can close every door instantly. When a threat is active, the Blue Agent takes on the manual investigation steps that usually eat an analyst's day: Is this activity legitimate, a security test, or an attack? What is the blast radius? Have our containment actions worked?

The Blue Agent goes beyond surface-level triage. It pulls together context from the Security Graph, code-to-cloud visibility, and runtime signals, and investigates the way a trained incident responder would. Specialized sub-agents answer the questions analysts would otherwise answer manually. For example, the Forensics sub-agent analyzes forensic evidence captured at detection time by the Wiz Sensor to uncover the root cause of suspicious activity and analyze what actually ran on a machine.

The Blue Agent shows its work: the questions it asked, the data it retrieved, and how each signal shaped the verdict. This ensures analysts can stay in control and trust the delivered verdict. With Wiz Workflows, teams can turn verdicts into action, automatically escalating incidents, notifying response teams, or triggering containment playbooks based on verdict and confidence level.

Agentic security for the SOC: proactive first, defensive always

Detection still matters, but it shouldn't be the first time you hear about a critical, validated, exploitable risk. With Red Agent and Blue Agent, your SOC has AI on both sides of the fight.

Get started with the Red Agent and Blue Agent, read the Red Agent and Blue Agent POV blog series, or book a live demo with our team.

articles.full_text:
At least nine AI Developer Platforms have disclosed incidents over the course of the month:

Fireworks AI (Oct 6)

Andromeda (Oct 9)

Zeabur (Oct 14)

Lightning AI (Oct 15)

OpenCode (Oct 16–17)

Railway (Oct 20)

Warp (Oct 23)

CommandCode (Oct 28)

Northflank (Oct 30)

Wiz customers can refer to our relevant Threat Intel Center advisories for more information on the Railway Platform Breach, Lightning AI Security Incident and the overall campaign.

Fireworks, OpenCode, and Warp have all reported indications of an “agent swarm” attack. Andromeda’s incident report calls it part of an "industry-wide attack." OpenCode and CommandCode have explicitly attributed their incidents to an attempt at “distillation.”

Any other month, and this would be the top security story. However, with all the ongoing incidents, few reports are connecting the dots across these attacks (Cloud Security Alliance as a notable exception).

The Pattern in these Attacks

Currently, most of these security incidents are still being analyzed, and detailed technical information is not available. Zeabur has shared a full write-up, and the company will be shutting down due to this incident. Railway has released a preliminary report and timeline.

However, there are some indicative details. Fireworks, Zeabur, and Lightning all attribute their incident root causes to credential access. Lightning was previously impacted by a supply chain attack within the Mini-Shai Hulud campaign. Railway so far has shared they believe the initial access was via “privilege escalation in our build infrastructure,” while Warp has suggested the root cause was a third-party vendor dependency, and OpenCode attributes it to a “legacy system.”

All public reports highlight targeted exploitation, explicitly hunting stored environment variables, with a focus on those granting AI access. While there is no single vulnerability or dependency linking these attacks, the overall picture is strongly aligned with recent reports on two fronts:

Agentic Attacks, which can enable threat actors to compromise victims faster and more efficiently.

The rise of LLMJacking, and the associated infrastructure of LLM Brokers. These create a market that makes the theft easily monetizable, likely driving more actors to undertake operations to steal credentials. Distillation, notably alleged against Chinese AI labs, drives demand as well.

Impact and Follow-on activity

Reports on the impact of these attacks have so far been limited to anecdotal reports on social media, which include:

Alleged theft of cryptocurrency, to the tune of ~$371,000, using crypto keys stored in Railway

Abuse of stolen AI access, such as those from OpenCode, resulting in consumer bills in the hundreds to thousands of dollars

However, Wiz has been able to observe downstream abuse of enterprise credentials, whose compromise we can attribute to one of these vendor breaches. We will discuss an exemplary pair of such cases.

In both cases, we see abuse of keys that previously were heavily used from the infrastructure of a compromised vendor.

They shared an identical first unauthorized activity, which happened within 30 minutes of the reported credential access within the vendor breach. It was a single InvokeModel from a residential IP address, in a one-minute sweep that tested stolen keys across multiple organizations. The call asked for Claude Fable 5.1, failed, and fell back to Opus 5.5, which worked.

In the days after this initial validation, both keys saw only a trickle of traffic: 14–120 calls a day from the same small Go client. The calls on the two keys ran in lockstep, about a minute apart. This indicates a single ongoing verification job checking that the keys remained valid.

Case A

Four days after the initial validation, a rotating proxy pool ran a catalog probe across dozens of addresses, sending one call per model across vendors: Amazon Nova, DeepSeek, gpt-oss, GLM, Kimi, Grok, GPT-6 Astra and older Claude models. Every call worked except Fable. A few hours later, a boto3 script on a residential address enumerated Bedrock and EC2 quotas. Twenty-two seconds after that, bulk traffic started from the same address. Within the next half hour, a second host mapped quotas and model availability across regions, making more than a thousand calls in under a minute.

The Flood

Over thirty hours, after which the key was remediated, the actor made approximately 800k Bedrock calls, and about 90% of them succeeded. The bulk ran first from the residential address and then, overnight, from a Level 3 hosting address. The key's policy allowed global.* cross-region inference profiles, and the actor routed every call through them. Because global routing spread the load across regions, only about 6% of calls were throttled. Traffic leaned heavily on Opus: Opus models were three quarters of successful calls, led by Opus 5 (36%), Opus 5.5 (22%) and Opus 4.8 (10%).

Case B

Unlike Case A, this key was restricted. Seven days after the initial validation, it surfaced in an apparent reseller pool. Over four hours, thousands of failed calls came from rotating hosting addresses, each active for about 15 minutes. The calls failed because the key's policy allowed Bedrock only through us.* cross-region inference profiles, and the pool requested global.*.

Early the next morning, a checker on a shared VPN exit identified the working us.* model IDs. Two hours later, a boto3 script on a Level 3 address retested global.* and us.* and enumerated Bedrock and EC2 quotas. It was the same script, down to the version string, that had probed Case A. Within minutes, the floodgates opened.

The Flood

Over thirteen hours, after which the key was remediated, that single Level 3 address made approximately 1.7 million Bedrock calls, with over a million successful. Nearly all of the rest were throttled: without global routing, the traffic ran into the account's regional quotas. Traffic was spread across a dozen Claude models and was less Opus-heavy than Case A. Opus 5.5, Sonnet 4.5 and Opus 5 made up three quarters of successful calls.

The Stolen Tokens

In both cases, the token usage profile resembles resold coding-agent traffic. A typical call sent only a handful of uncached input tokens, the signature of prompt caching, and got back a few hundred tokens of output. A long tail of calls carried tens of thousands of uncached input tokens, consistent with many different end users behind a reseller. At list price, these two cases alone likely ran up over $100k in usage.

What we see from these Attackers

Our research has been able to link the usage of the keys in the cases above overt reselling organizations. While we are not able to definitively establish the relationship between these reselling organizations and either the initial compromise or the “flood” token abuse documented above, the actors had access to the compromised keys and tested them from their infrastructure. The use of the keys by multiple actors suggests a robust market for this type of credential.

“momo” - Resale (and compromise?)

Wiz Research identified an actor centered around 23.106.46.239 who appears to refer to themselves as “momo” who had access to the keys used in Case A and Case B and is tied to an overt LLM resale site. Infrastructure linked to this IP address goes back to 2025 and has hosted multiple sites with titles related to LLM resale, including the site llm-routing.com which is currently active and advertises discounted access to frontier models, while accepting payment in USDT. This IP has also hosted an Artex landing page in mid-October and was publicly named by Zeabur as being part of their compromise. While we cannot definitively tie this operation to the “flood” of abuse documented above, the operator did have access to the stolen keys.

The site momo.skin resolved to 23.106.46.239 in early 2026 and another site tied via passive dns (direct.465415.xyz), used the title "Moの自建网盘" ("Mo's self-built cloud drive").

In March of 2026, this actor begins advertising LLM related services, hosting sites with titles such as "ChatGPT Team 席位兑换" ("ChatGPT Team seat redemption"), and "ChatGPT 号池管理" ("ChatGPT account-pool management").

On October 8, 2026, a subdomain (artex.nhhh.de) resolving to 23.106.46.239 hosted a page with the title “ARTEX — 自主渗透测试控制台" ("ARTEX — autonomous penetration testing console"). This is four days before Zeabur’s timeline identifying that IP address targeting their infrastructure (Oct 12 - 14).

In late October the 23.106.46.239 address conducts api key checks on the keys used in cases A and B and attempts a PutAccountDataRetention call using the Case B key.

“Xingjiabi” - a second resale hub

Wiz also identified a second resale operation that was leveraging stolen keys. This one is publicly available at xingjiabiapi.org where they offer access to a wide range of frontier models for discount prices. Infrastructure tied to this site (38.246.114.118) was identified conducting permission checks on the keys used in both cases A and B. In both cases the checks were conducted after the high volume abuse of the key from unrelated ip addresses had already begun, suggesting that there is an active resale market for these keys.

A subdomain of the main site, s3.xingjiabiapi.org resolved to 38.246.114.118 beginning on September 10, 2026. This 38.246.114.118 IP address enumerated the key used in case A, listing the inference profiles and models per region, paging through every bedrock quota. It also conducted a manual test of the key being used in Case B.

One interesting note about this actor is they seem to be attempting to guard against distillation. Their domain was snapshotted hosting a page titled “蒸馏检测监控” (Distillation behaviour detection) that was designed to score users across three categories and attempt to sort them into “high risk”, “watch” and “normal”. This may indicate that the attackers are attempting to avoid being associated with distillation, potentially due to that activity leading to accounts being suspended.

These IPs were used to test stolen keys and are suspected to be linked to LLM token abuse and resale. We do not have evidence that links them directly to the “Black October” attacks mentioned in this blog.
