Which actions should security teams take?

Organizations should prioritize the following mitigation and remediation measures:

Apply security updates: Upgrade affected Brotli libraries, Node.js runtimes, Python packages, Bun, Envoy Proxy, and Istio deployments to their respective patched versions or later supported releases.

Identify vulnerable cloud workloads: Inventory virtual machines, Kubernetes clusters, containers, serverless functions, API gateways, and application dependencies for vulnerable Brotli components. Prioritize internet-facing services and workloads processing untrusted compressed data.

Review application exposure: Identify applications that decompress Brotli-compressed HTTP requests, external HTTP responses, uploaded files, or other attacker-controlled content. Include indirect and transitive dependencies in the assessment.

Rebuild and redeploy affected workloads: Update container base images, dependency lockfiles, and bundled libraries. Rebuild and redeploy affected container images, restart running processes, and verify that patched components are loaded.

Implement temporary mitigations: Where immediate patching is not possible, consider disabling Brotli decompression or rejecting Brotli-encoded requests before they reach vulnerable components. Restrict untrusted compressed responses where feasible. These controls may reduce exposure but do not replace patching.

Strengthen monitoring and detection: Review WAF, application, and network logs for suspicious Brotli-compressed traffic, unexpected application crashes, and anomalous process behavior. Monitor affected workloads for indicators of exploitation.

Wiz customers can use the pre-built query and advisory in the Wiz Threat Center to search for vulnerable instances in their environment.

articles.title: ASPM in the AI Era Part 2: Prioritize Exploitable Risks with Code-to-Cloud Context
articles.context: For example: SCA: CVE-based findings are enriched with context from the NVD Vulnerability Catalog, real-time EPSS (Exploit Prediction Scoring System) probability scores, active...
articles.full_text:
In Part 1, we established how to centralize your AppSec tools, correlate assets, and map scanner coverage across repositories. Establishing visibility is an essential baseline, but once your connectors start streaming data into a single location, prioritization becomes the primary focus.

As highlighted in our recent State of SDLC Security 2026 report, AI’s primary impact isn't necessarily introducing entirely new risks. It's the amplification of existing ones through faster code generation, contributing to a wider attack surface area with less time for human review.

For lean AppSec teams, the real promise of ASPM lies in how it helps prioritize application risk across their enterprise. But, as we saw with the React2Shell example, prioritization requires context across the entire application lifecycle. AppSec teams must quickly distinguish between theoretical code flaws sitting on un-deployed branches and active vulnerabilities running on internet-facing workloads.

To transform raw scanner output into actionable risk, Wiz Code executes prioritization across two distinct layers:

Finding-level prioritization: Normalizing scanner data into unified schemas, actively enriching findings with threat intelligence and network reachability, and deduplicating identical alerts across overlapping tools.

Attack path prioritization: Using the Wiz Security Graph to connect code-level findings with live cloud runtime context, elevating isolated flaws into fully validated attack paths.

Let’s look at how to operationalize both layers in your environment.

Enrich, Deduplicate, and Prioritize Individual Findings

Findings from connected scanners populate into their respective domains in the Wiz platform. For example, SAST results flow into the SAST Findings tab, SCA results populate in the Vulnerability Findings tab, and Secret results show up in the Secret Findings page. You can easily filter any table by “origin” to isolate alerts from a specific tool. In the example below, we’re filtering vulnerability findings surfaced from a Snyk SCA scan.

From this unified baseline, Wiz executes multiple layers of prioritization to help AppSec teams focus on what matters.

Enrichment

Imported findings are enriched with domain specific context, turning generic alerts into prioritized findings. For example:

SCA: CVE-based findings are enriched with context from the NVD Vulnerability Catalog, real-time EPSS (Exploit Prediction Scoring System) probability scores, active exploit availability, and CISA KEV status. Our Threat Research team also denotes findings with active threats and writes complete advisories, so security teams have the latest insight on zero days.

SAST: CWE findings include code snippets so security teams have visibility into the location and context of weaknesses.

DAST: Wiz independently validates network exposure for the web applications with DAST findings using the Attack Surface Management (ASM) module. The ASM engine can be configured to run other checks such as secrets or sensitive data exposure checks from the perimeter on these newly created endpoints. Private-only addresses are marked differently so teams can prioritize findings with a real external attack surface.

Secrets: Wiz runs ingested secrets through databases to see if the secret was leaked, classifies secret types for understanding its impact, and assigns severities to the detected secrets based on threat research if the originating scanner did not provide any.

Deduplication

Security teams should not waste time chasing down multiple vulnerability findings for the exact same issue. When multiple tools scan the same codebase and produce duplicative vulnerability findings, Wiz can easily reconcile them.

Wiz labels one finding as "Representative" and the duplicates as "Duplicate." Teams can apply automated Ignore Rules scoped to duplicate findings, instantly eliminating redundant noise in reporting without losing the underlying scanner audit trail. So instead of generating individual tickets for each finding, teams can create one ticket to consolidate the findings.

Prioritize Exploitable Attack Paths

Traditionally ASPM has focused on aggregating findings and prioritizing risk using simple scoring. Wiz takes a different approach by correlating findings with additional risk on the Wiz Security Graph. This is where the platform moves from managing vulnerabilities to managing exploitable attack paths.

The Wiz Security Graph correlates multiple risk factors into a single Wiz Issue (identifying toxic combinations of risk). Critically, these controls run on your third-party findings exactly the same way they run on native Wiz findings. If you connect a scanner, its data instantly becomes part of your code-to-cloud attack path analysis.

What this looks like in practice

Let's look at how this context transforms a standard alert into a prioritized Wiz Issue. Imagine your Snyk integration flags a high-severity SAST finding (such as a remote code execution or command injection flaw) on a repository branch. In a vacuum, a developer might treat this as an urgent priority, or they might ignore it if they assume it is an internal tool.

The Wiz Security Graph evaluates the entire deployment lifecycle to uncover the actual risk. A single Wiz Issue might reveal:

The Code Flaw: A SAST finding from Snyk and a native Wiz SAST finding, both originating on the same repository branch.

The Build Artifact: That specific branch was built into a container image currently running in a production Kubernetes cluster.

The Exposure: The Kubernetes cluster is exposed to the internet via a public application endpoint.

Active Validation: An Attack Surface Management (ASM) finding confirms the endpoint is actively reachable from the outside.

Instead of manually piecing together four separate alerts across three different tools, Wiz draws the connection natively. Because these findings all resolve to the same underlying resource and represent the same attack path, they are surfaced as one unified, high-priority Wiz Issue.

Conversely, if that same SAST flaw was detected on a branch that never ships to a running cloud workload, it remains a low-priority finding—sparing developers from interrupting their sprint for a non-exploitable risk.

Manage security debt at scale

Not every finding may map to an attack path. But, lower-severity findings still represent real risk if left unaddressed. In Wiz, organizations can track and govern these findings through Posture Issues.

AppSec teams can create logical groupings of findings based on several criteria such as severity, project, code repository and more to build tailored campaigns for managing security debt. Teams can also define SLAs for remediation to align with organizational policies.

Up Next: Remediation and Automation at Machine Speed

Separating signal from noise is a massive win, but prioritization without rapid remediation is only half the battle. Once critical attack paths are identified, how do you ensure the right engineering team fixes them without slowing down release cycles?

In Part 3, the final instalment of this series, we’ll explore how to remediate at machine speed. We’ll cover how to leverage the Wiz Green Agent to generate tailored remediation plans in developer workflows and how to automate response with Wiz Workflows.

articles.title: ARTEX in the Wild: Storm-0940 Expands Targeting of IT and Software Vendors

articles.full_text:
Throughout October 2026, we identified an actor using tooling associated with ARTEX, an autonomous AI penetration-testing agent, to target multiple IT and software vendors. The activity focused on identity providers (Okta, Entra, Cognito) and abuse of Microsoft 365 integrations. We observed repeated attempts to uncover authentication bypasses, enumerate APIs, and access customer data (of the targeted vendors) across multiple environments.

Our observations overlap with Microsoft's recent report on ​​Storm-0940, a Chinese-state aligned actor - linked to the recent supply-chain attack involving stolen vendor credentials and downstream Microsoft 365 tenants.

However, we have additionally observed the same infrastructure, tooling, and attack patterns targeting the sector as a whole. Pivoting on identified TTPs and IOCs, we have also identified the same actor expanding their attempted supply chain compromises into other software sectors.

In this blog, we will describe the repeatable patterns and methodologies the ARTEX-using actor applied across multiple environments and cloud providers, with examples taken from real world attacks.

What is ARTEX?

ARTEX is an open-source autonomous penetration testing framework. A Chinese developer published it on GitHub in July 2026, and it won Baidu's "Agent+" red team challenge that September. In practice, an operator supplies a target and an objective. A planner agent then chooses the next step, worker agents run tools like nmap, curl, and Impacket, and every result feeds a shared graph of assets and findings.

Attackers picked it up within weeks. ARTEX artifacts surfaced in attacks on South Korean banks in late September and attacks on Japanese companies in October. Microsoft and Zscaler have since tied it to two separate actors. The developer made the tool closed-source on October 8. By then, the code had more than 12,000 forks.

A repeatable playbook

Across the investigated environments, we observed a consistent sequence of reconnaissance and attack attempts:

Map the application: Download JavaScript bundles, exposed source maps, runtime configurations, and Swagger/OpenAPI documentation to discover internal API routes and application functionality.

Probe authentication: Repeatedly initiate sign-in flows, manipulate OAuth callbacks and state parameters, test unsigned JWTs, and probe SSO and Microsoft 365-specific endpoints.

Attack identity providers and login flows: Password-spray corporate Okta and Entra ID environments, and target internal and proprietary application login pages.

Abuse account recovery: Repeatedly invoke password-reset, username-recovery, activation, and reset-token endpoints.

Test tenant isolation: Register accounts using disposable email addresses where possible, then manipulate predictable identifiers to probe for broken access controls and unauthorized cross-tenant data access.

Adapt to defense mechanisms: Rotate IP addresses when blocked, and constantly circulate user agents.

What it looked like in the logs

We analyzed these attack patterns using HTTP access logs collected via Wiz Agentless Workload Detection, alongside identity provider logs such as AWS Cognito events, Entra sign-in activity, and Okta authentication logs.

Targeting Internal Applications

The agent's first move across all observed instances of the attack was always to read the application itself. Requests like these showed up minutes after first contact:

GET /packs/js/main-3a9f...js.map GET /assets/config.json GET /env.js GET /swagger/?format=openapi

Not long after, it started calling internal API routes by name. The only place those route names appear is in the source maps it had just downloaded.

Account recovery got the same treatment. The agent checked which usernames existed, then hammered the reset endpoints:

GET /Account/ValidateUserName?UserName=admin POST /api/v1/Users/GeneratePasswordResetToken → 204 POST /forgot_password

Where it could sign up, it did, using a throwaway mailbox from a free temporary-email service. Then, it immediately tried to look at someone else's data:

POST /v2/register_user → 201 POST /confirm → 200 GET /company/1/logins → 403 GET /api/users/generate_redirect_link?role=admin → 401

Before every fuzzing run, it checked what a baseline "not found" response looked like:

GET /zzz-nonexistent-xyz123

Targeting OAuth Identity Providers

When probing Microsoft OAuth flows, the agent directly manipulated the callback endpoint by injecting fabricated authorization codes and malformed state parameters, while also attempting to bypass authentication using unsigned JWTs:

GET /sign_in/oauth/microsoft/callback?code=AAAA&state=notvalidb64!! GET /sso?jwt=eyJhbGciOiJub25lIn0.eyJlbWFpbCI6InRlc3RAdGVzdC5jb20ifQ.

That second token simply decodes to {"alg":"none"} and {"email":"test@test.com"}. The agent bombarded more than 60 variations of SSO routes with this payload in just two minutes.

On AWS Cognito, we observed patterns mirroring the account recovery abuse seen in proprietary apps. This activity was reflected in events like InitiateAuth, ForgotPassword, and ResendConfirmationCode. These requests originated from the same mix of user agents observed in earlier attacks, including benign-looking programmatic clients like boto and python-urllib.

The agent also attempted to provision new identities directly, invoking the AWS Cognito SignUp API while cycling through its pool of user agents.

Password Spraying

We also tracked a massive password spray campaign across many of the observed targets. The activity was IDP-agnostic, hitting both Entra and Okta, and displayed several unique, AI-driven characteristics.

The attacks targeted hundreds of users and were executed in highly coordinated bursts. Each burst featured:

Dedicated user agents: A unique user-agent string was assigned to each burst, distinct from those used in previous waves.

Precise timing: The median gap between authentication attempts was strictly one second.

Sustained execution: Individual bursts lasted anywhere from 20 to 60 minutes.

Role-based targeting: The agent primarily focused on accounts belonging to software engineers.

Repeated attempts: Some individual users were subjected to more than a dozen login attempts.

Relentless by Design

The activity was persistent and highly automated. Some sessions lasted 24–30 hours, and when IPs were blocked, new addresses appeared within minutes.

In one session, the agent cycled through a dozen variations of the same SSO endpoint (/sso, /sso/, /sso/login, /sso/jwt, /jwt/sso…), each with and without the same forged token, at a rate of about one request per second. When a login page started rate-limiting the activity, the agent simply switched to a different endpoint on the same host and carried on.

We observed more than 15 different user-agent strings across the victims:

Python-based clients and curl;

Truncated Chrome strings and headless browsers with seemingly random version numbers.

More distinctive, self-describing identifiers, such as ReconProbe/1.0.

This variety, combined with the consistent attack patterns and ARTEX-related indicators, helped us connect the activity across multiple organizations.

Although most of these attempts failed, the true threat lies in the methodology. While a human attacker is bound by time constraints and fatigue, an autonomous agent does not give up. It simply continues to iterate until it finds a single weak point.

A clearly agentic attack

None of the individual techniques observed are novel. However, together the agent behind this attack is illuminated. There are a few clear signals:

Steps were chained automatically: when sign-up was open, it registered with a disposable mailbox, confirmed the account, and immediately requested another company's data.

Each automated step used the output of the last one: internal API routes are called by name minutes after pulling the source maps

Adaptation was automatic: when a login page started rate-limiting, the agent moved to a different endpoint on the same host. When an IP was blocked, a new one appeared within minutes.

Not all attacks were logical: a human attacker of this skill level is unlikely to spend their time testing generic payloads on the heavily scrutinized Microsoft OAuth flows.

Staying Ahead of AI-Powered Attacks

As AI makes reconnaissance and exploitation attempts faster and easier to scale, defenders need to shorten the gap between exposure and remediation. Learn more about how to prepare with Wiz's AI Threat Readiness Framework.

In addition, Wiz's AI Red Agent continuously and autonomously conducts offensive tests, helping reduce exposure at the speed of AI - evening the scales.

Wiz customers can refer to our Threat Intel Center Alert: ARTEX: Agentic AI Campaign Enables Cloud and Supply Chain Compromise

Existing detection rules can also effectively identify this activity, for example:

Numerous Failed Login Attempts To Multiple Users Followed By A Successful Login To Admin User

Potential Password Spray Attack From Single IP

Okta Users Password Spray

The relentless behavior also creates predictable patterns that can also be detected by rules such as "Unusual Mass Access Denied Activity."

articles.title: PHP2Shell: AI uncovers critical RCE vulnerabilities affecting 70% of the Internet
articles.context: Core PHP engine flaws enable remote code execution and Heartbleed-style memory disclosure across the web.
articles.full_text:
Executive Summary

Wiz Research uncovered multiple critical vulnerabilities in core PHP, a popular general-purpose scripting language that powers 70% of all websites in the world. Successful exploitation could allow attackers to take control of affected servers, steal sensitive data, and deface the websites running on them.

PHP is a backbone of the web: it’s the programming language powering WordPress, Joomla, Drupal, Wikipedia’s MediaWiki, and many others.

These vulnerabilities include memory disclosure and unauthenticated remote code execution in PHP itself, independent of the application running on top of it, putting every affected website in immediate risk.

Every PHP version released in the last decade is affected by at least one of these vulnerabilities, going back to version 5.4. Attackers can exploit them remotely, in some cases fairly easily. Immediate patching is strongly advised.

On October 21, 2026, PHP released the patch fixing multiple memory-safety vulnerabilities in the core engine.

These findings rank among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history. The underlying flaws had been present for decades, but demonstrating their exploitability required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve. Frontier AI models substantially reduced that barrier, turning a longstanding flaw into an exploit.

Overview

In this post, we explain how frontier AI helped us find and fix vulnerabilities that had remained hidden in the PHP codebase for more than a decade. The issues described below all stem from key architecture decisions, some made over a decade ago, and were grouped under two CVEs, with severity reaching CVSS 9.2. The work grew into a cross-industry effort to protect customers, find variants, deploy detections and mitigations, and verify a patch in time for coordinated disclosure.

Nearly every PHP version is affected by at least one of these issues, including releases dating back to PHP 5.4. The vulnerabilities can allow unauthenticated attackers to execute code on affected servers or read sensitive process memory. That memory may contain passwords, authentication tokens, API keys and certificates belonging to other requests or the server itself.

PHP is the programming language behind much of the web, powering WordPress, Drupal and MediaWiki, the software that runs Wikipedia. A flaw in its core engine can affect websites across this ecosystem, even when their own application code is secure.

Some vulnerabilities become turning points because they challenge fundamental assumptions about security. In 2014, Heartbleed exposed the fragility of shared infrastructure securing the internet. In 2021, Log4Shell revealed how deeply embedded software dependencies could create widespread exposure that organizations struggled to identify. We believe PHP2Shell could mark a similar turning point for the AI era, illustrating how AI can change the practical exploitability of longstanding vulnerabilities. Building the exploit required chaining multiple flaws and adapting to each target’s memory layout through repeated testing and debugging. Frontier models were critical to making this process practical, enabling us to develop and adapt working exploits across multiple applications in hours. As the time and expertise required for this work decrease, complexity may no longer provide a meaningful barrier, changing how we define what is vulnerable in practice.

Wiz Research would like to thank the PHP team, Calif and OpenAI for their work on discovery, coordination and patch verification. OpenAI and Calif also published blogs containing details on the vulnerability – its history, technical details, and insight into the disclosure process. PHP posted as well.

We’d also like to express our sincere gratitude towards Automattic, Akamai, AWS, Cloudflare, Fastly, Google, Imperva, Microsoft, Vercel, and many others, for helping prepare guidance and out-of-the-box mitigations for customers who cannot apply the patch immediately.

The Vulnerabilities

All of the disclosed vulnerabilities are memory-safety issues that stem from bugs in how PHP handles fatal errors while processing requests, particularly out-of-memory errors. These bugs can leave a corrupted internal PHP state behind after a request ends unexpectedly. A later request or worker can reuse that stale state, leading to memory disclosure or corruption.

Below you can find a table that demonstrates what type of impact was demonstrated by each of the bugs we reported to PHP. The applications listed below are targets we chose for the RCE demonstrations. They are representative targets - exploitation does not require one of these CMSs, as the vulnerable code is in PHP itself.

Tracking ID

Bug

What an attacker can achieve

What we demonstrated

CVE-2026-109618

Upload-progress unserializer use-after-free

Remote process-memory disclosure

Corrupt process memory and execute code

Unauthenticated disclosure of PHP worker memory

Pre-authentication RCE on WordPress, Drupal and Joomla

Application-agnostic remote memory disclosure

CVE-2026-109619

Fatal-error backtrace use-after-free

OPcache type confusion

Corrupt process memory and execute code

Corrupt shared PHP state and execute code

Pre-authentication RCE on Drupal

Pre-authentication RCE on WordPress

While this blog covers only four instances of exploitable bugs (grouped under two CVEs) that follow this problematic pattern, there are other tracked, and likely untracked, variants of this issue in the PHP codebase. These variants have different requirements for exploitation and can lead to different types of impact. In any case, the patch provided by the PHP team fixes the issue at its core and eliminates all variants in the patched release.

Impact

We combined these vulnerabilities into a single exploit script, php2shell, and demonstrated that it could execute code remotely without authentication on deployments of WordPress (wordpress:latest), Drupal (drupal:latest), and Joomla (joomla:latest), using their latest container images at the time of testing.

These platforms illustrate the impact, but the vulnerabilities are in PHP itself. Exploitation does not depend on a flaw in the application’s code: even a simple “Hello World” application running on an affected PHP version can be vulnerable.

Separately, we demonstrated that attackers could read sensitive data from the PHP process’s memory, including passwords, tokens, and API keys, without needing to achieve remote code execution.

Demonstrations of PHP2Shell with Wordpress, Joomla, and Drupal:

The AI inflection point

The vulnerable code had been present for more than a decade. Turning these flaws into working exploits required chaining multiple bugs and accounting for how PHP allocates and reuses memory across requests. Memory bugs are notoriously complex; differences in PHP versions, configurations and application behavior can break assumptions the exploit depends on. An attack that works against one deployment may need substantial adjustments to work against another, each requiring further analysis, testing and debugging. Pre-AI, this manual work would be difficult to implement and even harder to scale.

With AI this is no longer a barrier. LLMs can help adapt an exploit to different PHP versions, configurations and memory layouts. With testing and debugging tools, models can analyze failures and iterate on adjustments, reducing the specialist effort required for each target. This significantly lowers the barrier to scaling attacks across different deployments.

This changes the economics of both discovery and exploitation. As AI reduces the effort needed to develop and adapt complex exploits, vulnerabilities that once seemed impractical to exploit become viable targets.

We used Wiz Atlas, Gemini 4 Argon and GPT-5.6 Sol throughout this research. Notably, Gemini 4 Argon made an invaluable contribution to finding the vulnerability, exploit development, attack detection, and validation of the patch.

Using Gemini 4 Argon, the team at Wiz has shown why frontier AI is a game-changer for cyber defense. For over a decade, these critical vulnerabilities remained unaddressed because vulnerability discovery and exploitation were incredibly complex. We're pleased to see Gemini 4 Argon help defenders bridge that gap, finding vulnerabilities and helping patch them.

Raluca Ada Popa, Head of Gemini Security, Google DeepMind

Industry-level collaborations

Prior to public disclosure, Wiz Research worked with the PHP team, Calif and OpenAI on discovery, coordination and patch verification. We also partnered with Google Cloud, Cloudflare, AWS, Microsoft, Automattic, Fastly, Akamai, Imperva, Vercel and many others to prepare customer guidance, detections and out-of-the-box mitigations for organizations that cannot update immediately.

A vulnerability in core PHP reaches far beyond a single application. PHP runs across clouds, hosting providers, content-delivery networks and millions of independently managed servers. Reducing exposure before the technical details became public required coordinated work across that entire ecosystem.

Technical deep dive

Bug: Upload-progress unserializer use-after-free

PHP's Session module can decode session data during upload-progress handling in the same pre-initialization window. The decoder stores request-owned bookkeeping in BG(unserialize). A fatal allocation failure can interrupt this path, destroy the request heap and leave the unserializer's global state published.

On a later request handled by the same worker, PHP can consume attacker-reclaimed memory as live unserializer bookkeeping. The stale state becomes a powerful memory-corruption primitive. We combined it with the memory disclosure to remove address uncertainty and achieved unauthenticated remote code execution on WordPress, Drupal and Joomla.

The WordPress, Drupal and Joomla chains are representative demonstrations. The underlying primitives exist at the PHP engine level and can affect any PHP application running on a vulnerable version.

These issues execute below the application layer, so application logs may contain little context. Until systems are patched, defenders should pay particular attention to unusual multipart requests followed by memory-limit errors or repeated HTTP 500 responses, unexpectedly large or malformed PHPSESSID response cookies, and unexplained PHP worker churn. These signals can guide an investigation. Applying the PHP security update remains the only complete remediation.

Bug: Remote process-memory disclosure

PHP parses RFC1867 multipart requests during request startup, before normal module initialization has completed. Session upload-progress handling can initialize Session state at this early stage and publish a session ID in PS(id). An out-of-memory error can abort the request before cleanup completes. PHP then destroys the request heap and may leave PS(id) pointing to the freed allocation.

A later multipart request handled by the same worker can reach the upload-progress cleanup path before normal Session initialization resets that pointer. PHP trusts the stale pointer and length as a live zend_string and URL-encodes the reclaimed heap contents into a PHPSESSID response cookie. The attack works even when the application never calls session_start(), making the issue application-agnostic. We demonstrated unauthenticated disclosure of an attacker-sized region of live worker memory containing data from outside the attacker's request.

Bug: Fatal-error backtrace use-after-free

In affected versions, PHP retains the backtrace of the most recent fatal error in EG(last_fatal_error_backtrace). A fatal out-of-memory error can destroy the request heap without undefining that executor-global value. The worker survives with a global that still points to memory from the previous request.

If the same worker emits a diagnostic early in the next request, it can access the pointer before the executor reinitializes that state. PHP then destroys or updates the dangling backtrace and follows attacker-reclaimed memory. The resulting cross-request use-after-free can be developed into controlled memory corruption. We demonstrated unauthenticated remote code execution against Drupal using this primitive.

Bug: OPcache type confusion

OPcache persists compiled PHP structures in shared memory and assigns indices into per-worker runtime-pointer maps. Workers coordinate those indices through a shared frontier. During zend_accel_script_persist(), PHP advances the process-local CG(map_ptr_last) frontier. It publishes the corresponding shared frontier only after persistence completes. An allocation failure between those two events leaves the process-local advance in place and partially persisted objects referring to slots that the shared state still considers available.

When another worker later reuses one of those slots for a different runtime object, stale shared metadata resolves to a pointer of the wrong type. The mismatch creates a cross-worker type confusion and corrupts shared OPcache state. We used this primitive to build an unauthenticated RCE chain against WordPress.

There are other variants outside of these four bugs. While we initially reported these four to PHP, through this research we realized the vulnerability is deeply rooted in the PHP codebase and will require a comprehensive fix. Other variants should also fold under the same two CVEs.

How Can Wiz Help?

Wiz customers should refer to the Wiz Threat Intel Center advisory for PHP2Shell, which includes built-in coverage for agentless and runtime vulnerability detection, exploitation detection via Wiz Defend and Sensor, and automatic response policies, alongside remediation and threat hunting guidance.

Sensor customers using the newest version (1.0.12768) can also enable a built-in response policy to automatically terminate processes exhibiting behaviors typical of PHP2Shell exploitation:

Conclusion

With 70% of the Internet affected, the impact of PHP2Shell cannot be overstated. It marks an AI inflection point. The vulnerable code had been there for more than a decade – what AI changed was the ability to understand the weaknesses and turn them into a working exploit. With frontier AI models and the right tools, a single researcher completed in a week what previously would have taken a world-class team months of work.

This changes the economics of both discovery and exploitation. Vulnerabilities that once seemed impractical to exploit become viable targets. These same capabilities also give defenders a chance to uncover and fix flaws that have survived years of scrutiny.

Wiz used Wiz Atlas, Gemini 4 Argon, and GPT-5.6 Sol throughout this research, with Argon making a particularly significant contribution to finding and helping to remediate the vulnerability.

The opportunity is to make this work routine: systematically finding flaws in existing software and catching new ones before they reach production. Our coordinated efforts with PHP, OpenAI and Calif advance that goal, applying AI to strengthen the software foundations we all share.

Responsible disclosure timeline

August 19, 2026: Wiz Research discovers the first PHP vulnerability using Wiz Atlas, Gemini 4 Argon, and GPT-5.6 Sol.

August 20, 2026: Unauthenticated RCE is confirmed against Drupal.

August 21, 2026: Unauthenticated RCE is confirmed against WordPress.

August 24, 2026: Wiz Research reports the vulnerabilities to the PHP security team.

September 21, 2026: PHP acknowledges the reports and begins developing a coordinated fix.

October 21, 2026: Patched PHP releases become available.

October 21, 2026: Public disclosure.

Stay in touch

Hi there! We are Sagi Tzadik, Shir Tamari, Nir Ohfeld and Tomer Schwartz from the Wiz Research Team (@wiz_io). We are a group of veteran white-hat hackers with a single goal: to make the cloud a safer place for everyone. We focus on finding new attack vectors in cloud software and uncovering isolation issues in the systems organizations depend on. We would love to hear from you on X or at research@wiz.io.

articles.title: LiteLLM Compromised, Steals Credentials
articles.context: We have not yet confirmed how the attacker gained access to our internal deployment, but currently suspect it was through a recently patched vulnerability
articles.full_text:
LiteLLM Compromised

At 11:39 UTC on October 21, a malicious version (1.107.0) of the LiteLLM package was uploaded to PyPI. This version was quarantined on PyPI as of 13:20 UTC. According to ClickPy data, the malicious version received approximately 49,000 downloads.

LiteLLM Docker containers on GHCR and Docker hub also included the trojanized version of LiteLLM. These included the v1.107.0 , latest, main-latest and main-stable tags. These were removed ~13:53 UTC.

The most recent safe version is v1.106.2.

When the malicious package is installed, three files are extracted directly into the site-packages root: cook.pth, cook.py and sitecustomize.py. These packages are designed to be executed whenever a python interpreter is started.

Per LiteLLM developer BerriAI:

malicious actions were taken through three engineers' GitHub accounts, appearing to be by way of stolen GitHub CLI OAuth tokens. The threat actor used one user's account triggered the project-releaser run, and another user's account to approve it. All tokens which were involved in this attack have been revoked.

And in a followup:

GitHub CLI OAuth token exposure After a thorough investigation, we have observed specific situations in which Claude Code will embed a user’s GitHub CLI OAuth token into a response body, and in situations where response bodies are logged, these tokens may appear in LiteLLM logs. Access to our internal LiteLLM deployment We identified an unexpected, innocuously named user account in our internal LiteLLM deployment, which was exposed to the public internet. We believe the attacker gained access to this deployment, obtained the GitHub CLI OAuth tokens from its logs, and subsequently used those credentials to compromise our release workflow. We have not yet confirmed how the attacker gained access to our internal deployment, but currently suspect it was through a recently patched vulnerability.

UPDATES

14:05 UTC - added IOC table

14:15 UTC - added Attack Commits details

14:40 UTC - added Credential Stealer details, noted Docker takedown

15:20 UTC - clarified dual-technique approach novelty and LLM-aided development

19:05 UTC - added observed post-exploitation activity

Payload

The payload has strong indications of LLM-aided development, including verbose variable names (encrypted_private_key_output), overly defensive error handling with generic try/except blocks, platform-specific code paths that fail silently on untested platforms (Windows marker path /tmp/ doesn't exist, fcntl/fork calls crash the remote loader), and a dead code module (exec_py) that was defined but never called. The structure suggests iterative prompting: functional on the happy path but brittle at the edges and untested.

Upon startup, the interpreter processes cook.pth, which includes a command to import cook, which loads cook.py. cook.py deobfuscates itself, runs a stealer routine and writes a maker to /tmp/.pc_once_72129118c59f5636c0bb (note this fails on Windows, as the /tmp/ path often does not exist). The stealer routine gathers system, browser, developer, cloud and AI tool secrets, encrypts them and exfiltrates to www.litellm.dev/healthcheck via a post request. This domain is attacker controlled, impersonating LiteLLM infrastructure.

Python interpreters will also attempt to execute sitecustomize.py - however, it will only run on Linux & MacOS machines. This script attempts to fetch domain.txt from a GitHub dead drop (letters9813/pythonclient-test/main/domain.txt). If it receives a response, it will attempt to download a second stage python script from http://<domain>/codepy and run it. As of the time of analysis, the domain.txt file was never populated beyond initial test values. The repo has been taken down by GitHub as of 1:30 PM UTC.

The dual-technique approach, using both .pth files and sitecustomize.py simultaneously, appears to be the first documented case in the wild.

Credential Stealer

The embedded credential stealer, internally named privcollect, harvests sensitive data across 16 modules targeting browsers, cloud providers, and AI services. It extracts:

browser credentials and cookies from Chrome, Firefox, Edge, and Safari

AWS credentials from ~/.aws/, environment variables, and EC2/ECS instance metadata (IMDS)

GCP service account keys and application default credentials

Azure tokens from the CLI cache

In terms of AI-specific theft, it targets API keys for OpenAI, Anthropic, Cohere, and other LLM providers stored in environment variables or config files. It also collects SSH private keys, GPG keys, and shell history files.

LiteLLM Proxy stores upstream API keys in a PostgreSQL database. The stealer queries this database directly (SELECT * FROM "LiteLLM_CredentialsTable" LIMIT 500) to extract all configured provider credentials.

Harvested data is encrypted with AES-256-CBC (key wrapped with RSA-4096) and exfiltrated over HTTP to www.litellm[.]dev/healthcheck using the hardcoded X-Token header and an Internet Explorer 7 user-agent string.

Attacker Commits

The payload originates with malicious commits made on github.com/Berri-AI/litellm. Note, this is a hyphenated variant of the legitimate BerriAI organization. This repository, not visible on GitHub, was used to inject the payload into the release pipeline.

Between 08:56 and 10:46 UTC on October 21, the attacker pushed 10 commits using the author email ckdi82fkoos@proton.me. The first nine commits were created on GitHub.com and therefore signed with GitHub's verified signature.

The first three (within 2 minutes) added the persistence files: cook.pth, cook.py, and sitecustomize.py. Four more commits bumped version numbers to 1.107.0.

After a 39-minute gap, two commits refined the payload and added the critical data = "cook" directive to pyproject.toml, which instructed the build tool to bundle the malware into the wheel.

A final commit, made 58 minutes later with a different email (Berri-AI@users.noreply.github.com) and unsigned (suggesting a different environment), added COPY cook ./cook to the Dockerfiles.

Although the Berri-AI repository is unavailable, all commits remain accessible through the parent repository due to Git's fork object sharing. The full diff is available at: github.com/BerriAI/litellm/compare/a8113b0d...20535d8f

Post-Exploitation Activity

Wiz Research has observed abuse of stolen credentials, starting approximately 4.5 hours post-exfiltration. Between 16:20 and 17:01 UTC, the attacker validated AWS instance role credentials harvested from compromised CI runners and Kubernetes nodes across multiple environments, from the following IP addresses:

168.100.8[.]57

165.227.201[.]8

Each credential was checked with sts:GetCallerIdentity, followed by bedrock:ListFoundationModels and a ListModels call, consistent with LLMjacking.

In a small number of environments, the attacker also enumerated IAM (ListRoles, ListUsers, ListAccessKeys) and performed general discovery (ListAccounts, DescribeTrails, etc.).

Recommendations

Wiz customers should review our Threat Intel Center advisory: Supply Chain Attack Targeting LiteLLM .

The Runtime Gap That Slows Teams Down

Containers have changed how modern applications are built and shipped, enabling rapid microservice deployments, agile CI/CD pipelines, and now high-performance AI workloads. But as clusters scale across environments, catching threats in production remains a major operational hurdle.

Static vulnerability scanners and pre-deployment image checks examine artifacts at rest. They are essential for catching setup flaws early, but they cannot stop active exploits, live reverse shells, privilege escalations, or zero-day execution paths unfolding in node memory.

The Wiz approach starts with agentless scanning, to build a continuous, full-stack view of your environment through the Security Graph. By correlating vulnerabilities with network exposure, identity permissions, and sensitive data access, Wiz maps critical attack paths and surfaces only the risks that truly matter, cutting through alert fatigue before a single line of runtime code runs.

But posture alone cannot stop active threats. You need runtime protection. Yet security and platform engineering teams have historically been caught in a frustrating trade-off:

Deployment friction: Manually orchestrating third-party Helm charts and manifests across dozens or hundreds of clusters creates an ongoing administrative tax.

Credential sprawl: Distributing and rotating registry tokens and API keys across individual namespaces introduces unnecessary risk and management overhead.

Governance blind spots: Newly provisioned clusters often go live without runtime coverage before security teams even realize they exist.

Performance anxiety: Platform leads worry that unbudgeted agent overhead will starve business-critical workloads of CPU and memory.

To eliminate this friction, runtime protection cannot be an afterthought. It must be native, platform-managed, and built directly into the cloud or hybrid environments’ fabric.

Announcing Native Wiz Runtime Protection on GKE

Today, Google Cloud and Wiz are excited to introduce the Wiz Runtime Sensor add-on for Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) in Preview.

Available directly within the GKE platform for both GKE Standard and GKE Autopilot clusters, this first-party integration transforms how teams deploy and manage in-cluster runtime security. Instead of manually managing third-party agents, GKE handles Wiz Sensor deployment, credential injection, and lifecycle updates automatically through the control plane.

Why This Integration Makes Runtime K8s Security Easier

Turn it on with 1 click: Enable runtime protection at cluster creation or on existing clusters with a single gcloud flag (--addons=WizSensor=ENABLED) or through the Google Cloud Console.

Zero credential distribution: Leveraging GKE’s native Secret Manager integration and Workload Identity Federation, API keys and pull tokens are vaulted off-cluster. Secret rotations in Secret Manager automatically resynchronize without requiring cluster restarts or pod redeployments.

Fleet-wide governance with Organization Policy: Platform security leads can mandate runtime protection across projects, folders, or entire organizations using custom Google Cloud Organization Policies. Unprotected cluster creation attempts are automatically blocked before workloads go live.

Predictable, kernel-level eBPF observability: Operating in kernel space via eBPF, the sensor monitors system calls, active processes, and network sockets with fixed per-node resource limits, safeguarding workload performance even under heavy traffic spikes.

Decoupled security updates: Sensor detection rules and threat definitions update independently of GKE cluster patch versions, node pool recreations, or workload maintenance windows.

Threat Detection in Action

Once active, the Wiz Sensor continuously monitors for high-risk runtime behaviors, including reverse shells, binary executions from /tmp, image drift, and privilege escalation attempts.

When an incident occurs, such as a container spawning an unauthorized interactive shell while modifying system files, the sensor flags the event instantly. Within seconds, a high-fidelity alert surfaces on the Threats page in the Wiz Portal, highlighting the exact pod, namespace, container image, and execution context.

articles.title: From Phishing to LLMjacking: Threat Actors Targeting Cloud Billing Accounts for LLM Usage
articles.context: Threat actors are not only using AI as a tool to conduct attacks, they are also compromising victim environments solely to abuse their finances for mass Large Language Model...
articles.full_text:
The Wiz Customer Incident Response Team (CIRT) has investigated a rising threat pattern in cloud environments: threat actors hijacking cloud billing accounts to fund unauthorized AI usage. Threat actors are not only using AI as a tool to conduct attacks, they are also compromising victim environments solely to abuse their finances for mass Large Language Model (LLM) execution, incurring hundreds of thousands of dollars in AI API charges.

Wiz CIRT has investigated multiple intrusions demonstrating this pattern, with this blogpost focusing specifically on campaigns targeting Google Cloud Platform (GCP) infrastructure. In these attacks, threat actors compromised privileged GCP user credentials and linked external, attacker-controlled GCP projects directly to the victim's internal billing accounts. Because the AI workloads were processed in foreign projects, prompt contents and model outputs remained completely hidden from the victim organization, leaving the nature of the mass AI usage unknown.

This blogpost details the full attack lifecycle observed across these intrusions, from the initial phishing and policy manipulation to cross-tenant project linking, and provides actionable threat hunting guidance to help organizations detect LLMjacking in their environments.

Initial Access: Phishing via Sponsored Search Ads

The attack began with a classic yet efficient phishing tactic. The threat actor purchased Google Search ads for common administrative search terms such as “google cloud” and “gcp”. When a user clicked the malicious ad, they were led through a Google Sites redirect to a fake Google login web page. Victim users with valid access to Google Console proceeded to input their account credentials and multi-factor-authentication (MFA) codes into the phishing page. The malicious site captured the user supplied credentials before seamlessly redirecting the user back to the legitimate Google authentication prompt. Forced to authenticate a second time, the user likely assumed the initial attempt was a minor glitch. In reality, the automated phishing kit immediately leveraged the harvested credentials to execute the first malicious login into the victim’s GCP environment from 212.73.134[.]136, the source IP address of the phishing kit. The threat actor then reauthenticated a few minutes later from a second IP address, which was later used for the rest of the GCP activity. Following reports of this activity, Google Ads has taken action to remove the malicious ad campaign.

Google automatically flagged the anomalous login attempt as suspicious and dispatched security alert emails to the user's inbox. However, to catch such intrusions early, organizations should not rely on user awareness alone, but ingest and monitor Google Workspace User Log Events for suspicious login flags and anomalous re-authentication triggers.

Persistence and Privilege Escalation: Disabling Guardrails and Externalizing Billing

Once inside the environment, the threat actor leveraged the compromised account’s excessive privileges to solidify their access, bypass organizational security controls, and prepare the billing architecture for external exploitation.

Enabling APIs and Minting Service Account Credentials

Rather than creating new infrastructure from scratch, the attacker targeted existing, low-usage GCP projects to:

Enable the Gemini API product

Create service accounts with Gemini API keys

Add the newly created service accounts to high privileged roles such as roles/ml.admin and roles/mcp.toolUser

Dismantling Organizational Policy Controls

To expand their reach without raising immediate alarms within internal domain governance, the threat actor deleted safety policies at the organization level, such as iam.allowedPolicyMemberDomains. This action removed the guardrail that restricts Identity and Access Management (IAM) membership to verified company domains, enabling external, personal accounts to be granted access as well as high-privilege permissions.

Inviting External Threat Actor Accounts and Elevating Privileges

With domain restrictions lifted, the compromised user account was leveraged to add external actor-controlled Gmail accounts directly into the organization's billing account.

The threat actor also assigned administrative roles to the compromised users or the external accounts, such as:

roles/recommender.billingAccountCudAdmin on GCP projects

roles/billing.admin on GCP billing accounts

The role roles/billing.admin granted full control over the billing account, including the ability to manage permissions, attach external projects, and alter payment settings.

Linking Foreign Projects for Mass Exploitation

The threat actor linked external GCP projects directly to the victim’s internal billing account. This move established a cross-tenant access, allowing all API requests executed in the threat actors external projects to be automatically charged to the victim's billing account while keeping prompt payloads invisible to internal log monitoring.

Defence Evasion: Geographic Blending and Admin Lockout

Once initial access was secured, threat actors employed defense evasion techniques designed to avoid triggering location-based security alerts and prevent security teams from regaining control.

In each of the intrusions investigated, Wiz CIRT observed that after the initial login, subsequent threat actor activity shifted to originate from IP addresses geolocated within each victim organization's headquartered country, even when this did not match the compromised user’s actual physical location.

Additionally, after securing administrative control, the threat actors demoted pre-existing internal billing administrators from their administrative roles down to read-only billing viewers. This modification stripped legitimate administrators of their ability to revoke permissions or detach rogue projects directly from the console.

Impact: AI Resource Abuse

The primary objective of these intrusions was non-destructive financial exploitation - leveraging hijacked cloud infrastructure to offload the costs of high-volume LLM inference. Across the observed cases, the impact manifested as rapid billing surges driven by automated, large-scale Gemini API utilization.

Within 24 to 48 hours of initial access, victim organizations experienced unexpected charges reaching tens to hundreds of thousands of dollars in unauthorized Gemini API usage. This activity represented a sharp surge from the organizations' established baseline compute spend.

Because the threat actors linked external, attacker-controlled GCP projects directly to the victim’s billing accounts, all API key generation, prompt requests, and model outputs occurred entirely within foreign tenants. Consequently, while the victim organization carried financial responsibility for the API consumption, internal security and audit logs provided no visibility into the nature, content, or context of the AI workloads being executed.

Detection and Threat Hunting Indicators

To detect potential LLMjacking and unauthorized billing account manipulation in your Google Cloud environment, security teams should hunt for indicators across Google Workspace, GCP Admin Activity, and Cloud Billing audit logs. Wiz customers can review the Threat Intel Center advisory that includes the following indicators:

Review Google Workspace and GCP audit logs for activity from the indicators of compromise section below. Wiz customers can use this Cloud Events query.

Review GCP IAM for any users with external domains, especially non-corporate email providers such as @gmail.com. Wiz customers can use this Cloud Events query, and replace the domain.com with their own organization domain.

Review GCP audit logs for changes to organization policy controls, especially allowedPolicyMemberDomains, and IAM policy changes related to billing account administrators. Wiz customers can use this Cloud Events query.

Review GCP audit logs for unexpected Gemini API enablement, service account creation and service account API key creation in old projects Wiz customers can use this Cloud Events query.

Monitor abnormal cost surge in API usage, and potentially enforce spend cap budgets. Wiz Cloud Cost customers can detect abnormal AI usage per model and cloud provider by monitoring Cost Monitor Findings for Resource Anomalies.

Wiz Defend customers ingesting cloud logs such as Google Workspace will get Wiz Threats on the initial logins. Customers ingesting GCP audit logs will get Threats for the described activity.

If you experience a breach or any cloud security incident, contact Wiz CIRT for incident response support.
