articles.title: Supply Chain Zero Days: Closing the Gap Between Publication and Detection
articles.context: By analyzing new npm package versions as they are published and distributing confirmed threat intelligence across the platform, Wiz helps teams identify compromised packages...
articles.full_text:
Modern software development depends on open source packages. Developers and AI coding agents can pull new dependencies and versions into projects at speed, helping teams build and ship faster.

But that speed creates a challenge for security teams. When a trusted package is compromised, malicious code can enter development environments and build pipelines before traditional vulnerability databases flag the threat.

Organizations cannot manually review or block every update to foundational packages without slowing development. Therefore, most organizations scan newly downloaded packages against known vulnerabilities and block if needed. But, zero-day supply chain compromises won’t show up in vulnerability databases right away; and, because popular packages are already trusted, developer workflows and build pipelines are often configured to automatically pull their latest versions. If an attacker compromises one of those packages, a malicious update can spread across the environment before a CVE is even published, leaving security teams to defend from behind.

Trusted package compromises in the wild

Our own research team is seeing this technique in practice more often than ever before. In H2 2025, notable supply chain attacks made up about 10% of significant incidents. In H1 2026, that percentage increased to 25%, and now, notable supply chain attacks account for 1 in 4 significant security incidents. During the Axios compromise, for example, an unknown threat actor compromised the npm account of an axios maintainer and published two malicious versions of the npm package (v1.14.1, v0.30.4), which introduced a dependency on plain-crypto-js, a newly created malicious package.

Although the malicious versions were removed within hours, that didn't mean that the threat disappeared. According to the Wiz Research team’s own observations, at the time, Axios was present in approximately 80% of cloud and code environments, and downloaded around 100 million times per week. The package’s popularity enabled rapid exposure, with observed execution in 3% of affected environments. This reality underlines the importance of speed in defending against supply chain attacks.

Detecting malicious packages at publication

Traditionally, security teams find out a trusted package was compromised by receiving a threat advisory or vulnerability database update. In an ideal world, teams could take a proactive approach to securing the software supply chain by knowing which packages published to npm are clean, preventing installation of those that are not, and alerting on malicious versions across all tools.

That’s why we built a dedicated supply chain detection pipeline to analyze new packages and versions as soon as they are published to npm. This allows us to flag malicious packages and add detection rules in Wiz Defend, code and cloud pipelines, all before a formal CVE is published.

Here’s how it works:

When a new package version is released, the pipeline downloads and extracts the current version and previous versions for comparison.

Static analysis techniques flag suspicious files. This analysis feeds into our AI classifier engine, which returns an initial verdict.

Suspicious versions undergo dynamic analysis to validate the verdict. This dynamic analysis involves in depth work to understand the file contents, including:

Installing the package version in a sandbox environment to monitor runtime activity.

Importing the version and exposed modules .

Running the package from the CLI (where possible).

The Wiz Sensor observes runtime behavior to monitor for malicious activity. This helps the pipeline confirm the suspicious verdict, and provides our AI classifier with additional evidence.

The AI classifier returns the final verdict, generated based on all previous analyses. Once a version is confirmed as malicious, the pipeline automatically publishes IOCs to the Wiz reputation service. This ensures that Wiz customers are alerted as soon as a package enters their environment, via:

Threat intelligence center notifications, alerting on compromised packages so teams can understand if they are impacted.

Code and cloud scanning pipelines, surfacing malicious package findings wherever detected.

Wiz Defend, with auto-updated detection rules for malicious packages and configurable runtime detection and response policies.

Combining various analysis methods and live runtime execution allows us to flag zero-day compromises at speed while keeping false positives to a minimum.

Detection in the real world

A notable example of the pipeline in action is the keyv attack, where multiple npm packages in the keyv/cacheable ecosystem were compromised following the compromise of a GitHub maintainer account. In this particular case, instead of hardcoding command-and-control (C2) domains into the package source code, where static rules could easily extract and block them, the malware dynamically retrieved its C2 domains at runtime by querying an Ethereum smart contract. Because the malicious domains never appeared in the code itself, traditional static analysis alone could not identify the C2 infrastructure.

Using the supply chain pipeline, the Wiz Research Team was able to successfully see network activity to the malicious domain, automatically detecting the malicious domain connection without human intervention. Combining static and dynamic analysis, along with AI classification and live runtime monitoring, helped the pipeline flag the package with high confidence. As soon as the package was confirmed malicious, the relevant information automatically pushed to Wiz Defend and across the Wiz platform, enabling customers to detect compromised keyv versions in their environments before a formal CVE was published.

Proactive detection of compromised packages with Wiz

Open source packages are fundamental to the modern software development ecosystem. As workflows accelerate, security teams need real-time visibility and control over third-party dependencies before malicious code can land on developer workstations or build pipelines.

By analyzing new npm package versions as they are published and distributing confirmed threat intelligence across the platform, Wiz helps teams identify compromised packages before traditional vulnerability signals become available. In addition, Wiz evaluates dependencies during each install or upgrade process, to help security teams detect and manage risky or compromised package versions at the exact point of ingestion.

The goal is simple: empower security and development teams to move at machine speed, with the visibility and control over what enters the software supply chain.

articles.title: Loud, Fast, and Everywhere: Anatomy of a Real AI-Driven Cloud Attack
articles.context: This blog post first examines the characteristics that set AI-driven attacks apart from traditional, human-operated intrusions
articles.full_text:
Over the past few weeks, the Wiz Customer Incident Response Team (CIRT) has seen a clear trend across investigations: AI-driven attacks are on the rise. In several recent intrusions, an AI agent system wasn't just assisting an attacker behind the keyboard. It was running the entire operation. It found entry points, harvested credentials, pivoted across platforms, and debugged its own scripts on the fly, driving the campaign from start to finish.

These intrusions don't look like traditional campaigns. They are loud, move at machine speed, and touch every layer of the cloud stack. The challenge for defenders isn't that these attacks are invisible. It's that their footprint is fragmented across identity providers, cloud control planes, CI/CD systems, and workload logs, and no single alert tells the full story.

This blog post first examines the characteristics that set AI-driven attacks apart from traditional, human-operated intrusions. It then walks through real-world examples from Wiz CIRT investigations. Finally, it outlines what security teams need in place to detect and respond to machine-speed attackers.

Characteristics of AI-Driven Attacks

AI-driven attacks behave differently from both human-operated intrusions and traditional script-automated attacks. While scripts execute pre-programmed steps blindly and human operators move slowly and sequentially, AI agents combine machine speed with contextual reasoning. Across multiple investigations, Wiz CIRT has observed a recurring set of characteristics that distinguish them.

Operational tempo - Activity can reach hundreds or thousands of actions per hour and continues for long periods without the pauses or working-hour patterns typical of a human operator.

Simultaneous activity across multiple platforms - The agent operates in several environments at the same time. While one task enumerates cloud resources, others deploy Kubernetes workloads, create CI/CD pipelines, or query databases, all from the same source and within the same time window. A human operator typically works through one environment at a time, and traditional scripts rarely cross environment boundaries simultaneously.

Proficiency across platforms - The AI agent uses the native APIs and tooling of each platform it reaches, including cloud providers, container orchestration, CI/CD systems, databases, identity providers, and message queues. Human operators rarely have deep working knowledge of all of these at once.

Credential chaining across environments - Because the agent has native fluency across so many technologies, every credential becomes a stepping stone to the next platform. For example, a Kubernetes service account token leads to a cloud service account, which leads to a CI/CD system, which ultimately grants full administrative access.

Rapid trial and error - While attackers have relied on scripts for years, when a script breaks, fixing it takes time. When an agent runs the operation, that entire feedback loop happens in real time. If an attempt fails, the agent immediately reads the error, rewrites its script on the fly, and tries again within minutes, with each new attempt directly fixing what broke the previous one.

Security-testing naming conventions - Resources, files, and payloads created by the actor are consistently labeled with terms such as pentest, probe, recon, redteam, and exfil. This framing likely helps the actor present the activity as authorized security testing, effectively bypassing the AI model’s safety guardrails.

Numeric task identifiers - Many of the resources, users, and files created during the attack include a numeric identifier, and the same number often appears across several related artifacts. Failed attempts are retried under the same number with a letter suffix (for example, -b, -c, -d). These identifiers appear to be internal task IDs that the AI agent uses to track its own work.

Generated code patterns - Human attackers rarely add comments to short-lived exploitation scripts. Code recovered from these attacks commonly includes descriptive headers and numbered step-by-step comments, and the same helper functions are reused across dozens of payloads. Both are a direct result of how the code was generated by the model.

Inside an Investigation: What an AI-Driven Attack Looks Like in Practice

AI-driven attacks don't follow a clean, linear path. The agent works across many platforms in parallel and loops back whenever new access opens up, so a traditional timeline doesn't capture how the attack unfolded. Instead, this section walks through key phases from an AI-driven attack investigated by Wiz CIRT, highlighting where the characteristics described above came into play.

The target was an organization with a large multi-cloud environment. The AI agent operated from several attacker-controlled IP addresses and moved across nearly every layer of the environment: cloud providers, Kubernetes clusters, CI/CD and GitOps pipelines, the identity provider, secrets management, data warehouses, and internal applications. Throughout the attack, it harvested credentials and secrets, accessed sensitive data, and used a variety of channels to move that data out of the environment.

Initial Access: Trying Every Door

Over the course of the attack, the threat actor probed multiple internet-facing services using different techniques. It sent exploitation payloads for well-known vulnerabilities, attempted anonymous access to cloud storage, and worked through the API of an exposed internal developer tool. There it tried to create an administrator account, trigger password resets, read local files through path traversal, and upload a test file named with a pentest prefix.

One of the confirmed initial access vectors was a Java remote code execution vulnerability in an exposed Kafka UI instance. Shell commands were spawned from the application's Java process, followed by malware deployment and the establishment of a C2 channel.

Even after gaining a working foothold, the agent never stopped scanning: it continued probing for alternative entry points in parallel to secure redundant paths into the network. Notably, the same source IP address was observed scanning across more than 600 other Wiz customer environments during the same window, consistent with broad, opportunistic automation.

Foothold Inside Workloads

Once the agent had code execution on an exposed endpoint, it pursued three goals almost immediately:

Maintain Access - Deployed backdoors and C2 agents to multiple pods across several clusters.

Harvest Credentials - Extracted mounted Kubernetes service account tokens, searched environment variables for strings such as token, secret, key, and pass, and queried the Instance Metadata Service (IMDS) to harvest credentials from the node's attached cloud service account.

Map Internal Reachability - Scanned internal message brokers, schema registries, and databases to determine which services could be reached from inside the pod's network namespace.

These harvested credentials became the primary entry point for lateral movement into the cloud control plane.

Operating in Cloud Control Plane

The agent operated in both of the organization’s cloud environments, GCP and AWS, at a tempo no human operator could match. Using access keys and service account credentials obtained from earlier parts of the attack and identity impersonation, the agentic attacker first conducted broad reconnaissance.

In GCP, it weaponized a service account provisioned with token-creation privileges, turning it into an automated minting engine that generated credentials across dozens of identities in rapid succession. In parallel, the agent scraped container registries in a continuous loop, attempted to exfiltrate high-value database records, and deployed publicly accessible Cloud Run services prefixed with pentest-.

Simultaneously in AWS, the agent leveraged AWS Systems Manager (SSM) to execute commands across instances in the environment. Through SSM, it attempted to connect to databases using harvested credentials, moved laterally via SSH, gathered additional secrets, and staged exfiltration to a bucket named pentest-<task_id>. To establish cross-account persistence, it created a new IAM user prefixed with probe and used it to assume OrganizationAccountAccessRole, gaining administrative access across member accounts in the AWS Organization.

Identity Provider: Becoming an Insider

Rather than relying only on stolen credentials, the agent created an identity of its own. Using a compromised administrator API key for the organization's identity provider (IdP), it made changes programmatically: creating a user with a pentest prefix, setting its password, activating the account and adding it to the administrators group.

When the IdP returned errors during the process, the agent troubleshot and worked through each failure on the fly. With a working identity in place, it expanded its blast radius through group memberships. It added the user to cloud role groups mapped directly to AWS IAM Identity Center roles, followed by broad organizational groups that granted inherited access across enterprise applications. Within minutes of the final group change, the newly minted identity was signing in to AWS through single sign-on (SSO), maintaining continuous authentication sessions until the account was suspended.

Weaponizing CI/CD and GitOps

CI/CD and GitOps platforms became the agent’s primary execution engines. Five distinct workstreams ran simultaneously, each one's output feeding the others:

Secret harvesting - harvested secrets from every source it could reach: the CI/CD platform's own secret store, Kubernetes Secrets and ConfigMaps, runner environment variables, cloud metadata endpoints, vault sidecars, Docker image layers, and databases opened by other workstreams.

Reachability mapping - deployed reconnaissance scripts to runners and pods to determine what each one could reach and what identity it carried.

Credential spraying - combined the output of the first two workstreams, trying harvested credentials against the reachable targets the agents managed to find: databases, cloud APIs, internal OAuth services, Kubernetes clusters, payment endpoints.

Service exploitation - researched accessible services to understand how they worked, what authentication flows they expected, and attempted to use them.

Compute expansion - deployed new runners and pods, moved laterally through SSH keys and native remote execution tools, and fed each new position back into the other workstreams.

The moment a new credential appeared it was tested against all known targets until access was confirmed, and the moment a new target became reachable, all known credentials were tested against it.

The agents didn't spray credentials blindly. They used context from earlier workstreams to pick the right runner for each operation. Once they learned a specific runner could reach a target, every subsequent operation against that target was routed through that runner. When a new credential appeared from a completely different source, it was automatically tried from the runner already known to reach the relevant environment.

Pipelines and manifests carried names like pentest_exfil, recon, foothold, dump-remaining, and harvest, with numeric task identifiers. Failed attempts were retried under the same identifier with a letter suffix, and the code inside each payload was structured with step-by-step comments and reused helper functions.While the two platforms offered different infrastructure and execution models, the same workstreams ran across both.

On the CI/CD platform, the agents used a compromised service account to create pipelines and leveraged existing runners for their reachability across different clusters, cloud accounts, and VPCs. The runners' own output logs served as the exfiltration channel for both secrets and data. For lateral movement, they used SSH keys and cloud access keys found through the secret harvesting workstream to reach hosts beyond the runners through SSM and other native remote execution tools.On the GitOps platform, the agents used a compromised deployment service account to push malicious Kubernetes manifests that the GitOps controller synced directly into the production cluster as running pods. The first manifest escalated to cluster-admin, and from that position the same workstreams ran inside the cluster.

Living Off Kubernetes

Kubernetes (K8s) played a major role in this attack, and not by coincidence. GitOps controllers run inside K8s clusters by design, CI/CD runners frequently run as K8s pods, and a large share of the secrets stored in CI/CD secret managers are themselves K8s tokens. The agent reached the K8s API through three separate doors: CI/CD runners, GitOps deployments, and the backdoor identity it had created in the identity provider.

The agent dumped secrets across multiple clusters, extracting database connection strings, OAuth client credentials, TLS certificates, and cloud service account keys. When role-based access controls (RBAC) blocked secret access, it pivoted to K8s ConfigMaps, finding hardcoded default passwords, plaintext credentials, and encryption keys. It executed remote commands inside running pods to read environment variables, and queried the instance metadata service to turn pod identities into cloud credentials.

After escalating to cluster-admin and granting itself unrestricted access across the entire cluster, the agent minted service account tokens to impersonate legitimate applications and attempted to authenticate to the organization's secrets vault as those applications. It also attempted to access vault-agent sidecars, helper containers that pull secrets from the vault and store them as plaintext files inside the pod, trying to read the decrypted credentials directly from the filesystem.

The cluster also became a persistence layer. The agent deployed a command-and-control implant as a self-healing Kubernetes workload, ensuring the backdoor persisted even if the pod was killed. It later modified running workloads by talking to the GitOps controller directly, leaving no trace in the Git history.

Data Access and Exfiltration

Data collection and exfiltration ran continuously throughout the attack, adapting to the channels that were permitted in each environment. It posted results to the request-catcher service webhook[.]site, committed dumped data to a repository in the organization's own source control platform, and staged output in a Kubernetes ConfigMap it created for that purpose. It also tried to create storage buckets named after the task, such as pentest-<task-id>-<objective>, as a destination. Those attempts were denied. When one route failed or hit a size limit, it moved to the next.

Below is a snippet of a script used during the exfiltration phase showing the agent's descriptive task comments:

#!/bin/sh # redteam <database> reader + cluster-admin foothold exfil (intent <task-id>)

The script queried the database's structure, searched column names for sensitive terms, and uploaded the results to webhook[.]site, along with the pod's own service account token "for future foothold reuse".

Recommendations for Defenders

AI-driven attacks are noisy, but noise only helps defenders who can see all of it, connect it, and act on it quickly. The following recommendations focus on closing the gaps these attacks exploit.

Unify logs across all platforms:

Every phase of this attack appeared in a different log source, and no single one told the full story. Cloud audit logs, Kubernetes audit logs, runtime events, identity provider logs, CI/CD audit trails, and SaaS application logs need to be collected and searchable in one place, with consistent retention. When logs are unified, defenders can connect activity across platforms and understand the full scope of an incident in minutes instead of days.

Wiz Defend offers real-time ingestion of various log sources including version control logs, cloud logs, identity provider logs, and more, as well as built-in threat detection rules to identify active threats in your environment.

Use AI for investigation and triage:

When an attacker generates thousands of events across diverse platforms, investigating alerts individually becomes impossible. Security teams should use AI-assisted investigation to group related alerts, summarize activity across sources, decode payloads, and highlight the most critical paths, so analysts can focus on decisions instead of manual correlation. It is important to act fast on true-positive incidents.

Wiz Defend is using context-aware grouping to correlate multiple detections from different log sources into a single coherent story based on the Detection context and time.

Wiz’s Blue Agent can assist with rapid investigation and triage - it is an AI-powered SOC investigation agent, and it is designed to autonomously investigate threats.

Assume full exposure on compromised resources:

In the case of a true-positive incident at this scale and speed, prioritize rotating all credentials on compromised resources rather than trying to trace exactly which ones were read. Document all secrets that were accessible from those resources, map each secret to its identity and hunt those identities and resources for any anomalous usage after the time of compromise.

Wiz's secret scanner can map the secrets on a specific resource, tie them to identities, and validate whether they are still valid.

Maintain endpoint and workload visibility:

AI agents tend to leverage endpoints directly, not just cloud API keys. They access internal services, connect to databases, deploy command-and-control agents, probe APIs, and move laterally from within runner pods, virtual machines, and containers. This activity doesn't appear in cloud control plane logs. Without runtime visibility on the endpoints themselves, including process execution, network connections, and file access, this activity would be invisible and impossible to remediate.

Wiz's Sensor can detect active processes, network connections, and runtime behaviors on a specific resource, tie them to workloads and identities, and alert on suspicious activity.

Wiz's Agentless Workload Detection provides visibility into critical assets where traditional agents cannot be deployed, like virtual appliances, vendor-managed systems, or workloads with strict performance requirements.

Restrict trust between different systems:

AI agents treat all different environments as a single one. Security teams must enforce strict isolation boundaries between environments. For example, a staging workload shouldn't be able to reach production credentials, a CI/CD pipeline shouldn't hold standing access to every environment, and a single service account shouldn't be able to create tokens for any other identity.

Wiz’s Security Graph can help detect attack paths and over-privileged identities to perform such lateral movement between environments.

Continuously scan the external attack surface:

AI agents scan broadly and quickly for any exposed attack path. It is therefore critical to discover and assess internet-facing assets, including developer tools, management consoles, and internal applications, and fix or remove exposures before an attacker finds them.

The Wiz Red Agent can detect attack paths in your environment. The Red Agent is an AI-powered security agent that acts as an intelligent attacker to discover and validate exploitable risks across your web applications and APIs.
